m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Install Python 3.10 or newer and check its version from a terminal.
  • Install VS Code and the Python extension, and say what job each one does.
  • Run a setup-check script from VS Code and read what it tells you.
  • Fix the four install problems that catch most people.

Two students run the same test file. One sees 2 passed. The other sees No module named pytest. The code is identical, so the difference has to be the setup: which Python ran the file, and whether that Python could see the testing tool.

This course is about designing programs out of classes, and you will lean on tests to know your designs still work. That only goes well if your setup is predictable. This module gets you to one editor, one Python per project, and one command that runs every test. This first lesson covers the installs.

#Three programs with three different jobs

It is easy to think "VS Code" is the thing that runs Python. It is not. Three separate pieces work together, and knowing which is which makes every later error message easier to read.

  • VS Code is a general editor. Out of the box it knows nothing about Python.
  • The Python extension (by Microsoft) teaches VS Code to run, debug, and test Python. It installs two helpers with it: Pylance, which powers autocomplete and type checking, and the Python Debugger.
  • The Python interpreter is the program that actually executes your code. You install it yourself; neither VS Code nor the extension includes it.

You need Python 3.10 or newer. Later modules use type-hint syntax like int | None, which older versions reject. Any current release from python.org is fine.

#Step 2: Install VS Code

Windows

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com (opens in a new tab) and download the Windows installer.
  2. Run it. On the Select Additional Tasks screen, leave Add to PATH ticked so the code command works in terminals. If the installer also offers GitHub Copilot CLI, you can decline it; this course doesn't use it.
  3. Open VS Code from the Start menu.

macOS

  1. Download VS Code for macOS from code.visualstudio.com (opens in a new tab).
  2. Open the download and drag Visual Studio Code.app into your Applications folder, then open it from there.
  3. Optional but handy: press Cmd+Shift+P, type shell command, and run the Shell Command: Install 'code' … in PATH entry. Now code . in Terminal opens the current folder.

Chromebook / Linux

  1. Find out which processor you have by running dpkg --print-architecture in the Terminal. It prints amd64 (download the x64 build) or arm64 (download the ARM64 build).
  2. From code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab), download the matching .deb package.
  3. Install it from the Terminal, in the folder where it downloaded (on a Chromebook, first move it into Linux files using the Files app):
  1. Open Visual Studio Code from your Linux apps.

#Step 3: Add the Python extension

  1. In VS Code, open the Extensions view with Ctrl+Shift+X (Cmd+Shift+X on a Mac).
  2. Search for Python.
  3. Pick the one published by Microsoft (its ID is ms-python.python) and select Install.

Several look-alike extensions exist. The Microsoft one is the one every instruction in this course assumes.

#Step 4: Prove the three pieces are connected

Use File › Open Folder… to create and open a new folder called oop-python. You will keep everything for this course in it. In the Explorer, select the New File button, name the file check_setup.py, and paste this in:

Save it (Ctrl+S or Cmd+S) and select the Run Python File play button at the top right of the editor. A terminal panel opens and prints three lines.

The output above came from the computer that built this page. Yours will show your own version and a path on your machine. The second line is the useful one: it names the exact interpreter VS Code used. When a package seems to be "missing", comparing that path with the one in your terminal usually reveals two different Pythons.

🧪 Try it yourself

Click the Python version shown near the bottom right of the VS Code window (the Status Bar). A list of every Python VS Code found on your computer appears. Close it with Escape for now; you will use it in the next lesson.

#The four problems people actually hit

⚠️ Windows: "python is not recognized", or the Microsoft Store opens

Windows ships with placeholder python shortcuts that open the Store. Open the Start menu, search Manage app execution aliases, and make sure the Python (default) aliases are switched on (if they are, switch them off and on again). Close every terminal and open a new one, since terminals only read your PATH when they start.

⚠️ macOS: `zsh: command not found: python`

macOS has no python command. Type python3. Inside an activated virtual environment, which you make next lesson, plain python works too.

⚠️ VS Code can't find Python, or asks you to select an interpreter

VS Code was probably open while you installed Python, so it never saw it. Quit VS Code completely and reopen it. If it still can't find Python, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P) and run Python: Select Interpreter.

⚠️ Chromebook or Linux: `Unable to locate package python3-venv`

Your package list is out of date. Run sudo apt update and then repeat the install line.

#Watch the setup once

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You install VS Code and the Python extension on a new laptop, but not Python. What happens when you press Run Python File?

  • The extension adds Python support to the editor but contains no interpreter.

  • VS Code and the extension only hand your file to a Python interpreter, and none is installed yet.

  • Pylance reads your code to give autocomplete and warnings; it never executes it.

Show answer

B. VS Code and the extension only hand your file to a Python interpreter, and none is installed yet.

2check_setup.py prints Running from C:\Python39\python.exe and Too old. What is the best next step?

  • The course needs features from 3.10, so the script is right to complain.

  • VS Code isn't the problem; it ran an old Python it found.

  • The path shows VS Code chose an old interpreter. Install a newer one and point VS Code at it.

Show answer

C. The path shows VS Code chose an old interpreter. Install a newer one and point VS Code at it.

Key takeaways

  • VS Code edits, the Python extension connects, and the interpreter runs. You install all three.
  • Use Python 3.10 or newer. On macOS and Linux the command is python3 until a virtual environment is active.
  • sys.executable tells you exactly which Python ran your file, which is the first thing to check when a package seems missing.
  • Most install errors are fixed by opening a fresh terminal or a fresh VS Code window.

  • Using Python on Windows (opens in a new tab): the install manager in detail, with a troubleshooting table for every Windows symptom.
  • Set up Linux on your Chromebook (opens in a new tab): Google's steps for turning on the Linux development environment.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a virtual environment in your project folder and point VS Code at it.
  • Install pytest with python -m pip so it lands in the right Python.
  • Write test functions that pytest can find, and run them from the terminal.
  • Read a failing test report and use it to find the problem.

By the end of this page your terminal will print 2 passed. Then you will break one test on purpose and read exactly what pytest tells you, because a failing test is far more useful than a passing one when you are learning to read it.

#Why every project gets its own Python

When you run pip install pytest, the package goes into whichever Python pip belongs to. Most computers end up with more than one Python, so it is easy to install a package into one and run your code with another. That is the No module named pytest mystery from the last lesson.

A virtual environment fixes this. It is a folder (by convention named .venv) inside your project that holds a private Python and its own package shelf. Install pytest while the environment is active and it goes on that shelf, and nowhere else.

The environment is disposable. If it ever gets into a strange state, delete the .venv folder and make a new one in ten seconds. Never put your own code inside it.

#Step 1: Create the environment

Open your oop-python folder in VS Code (File › Open Folder…), then open a terminal with Terminal › New Terminal. The terminal starts inside your project folder. Run:

Windows

macOS

Chromebook / Linux

A .venv folder appears in the Explorer. If VS Code pops up a message offering to use the new environment for this workspace, choose Yes. You can also do this whole step from the Command Palette with Python: Create Environment, then Venv; either way you end up with the same folder.

#Step 2: Select it and activate it

Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac), run Python: Select Interpreter, and pick the entry whose path includes .venv. Then close the terminal (the trash-can icon) and open a new one. VS Code activates the selected environment in new terminals, and the prompt starts with (.venv).

If you don't see (.venv), activate it yourself:

Windows

macOS

Chromebook / Linux

Now prove it. Save this as where_am_i.py and run it with the play button:

The output shown here came from the machine that built this page, which is not inside a virtual environment, so it says False. Yours should say True, with a path ending in .venv/bin/python (macOS, Linux) or .venv\Scripts\python.exe (Windows). Inside an environment, sys.prefix points at .venv while sys.base_prefix still points at the Python it was made from, so the two differ.

#Step 3: Install pytest

With (.venv) showing, run:

The second line should print something like pytest 9.2.0. Notice the commands start with python -m. That runs pip and pytest as part of this exact Python, so they can't wander off to a different one. Once the environment is active, python means the environment's Python on every operating system, including macOS.

#Step 4: Write a test pytest can find

Create test_first.py in the project folder:

Running this file directly prints nothing at all, which is why there is no Output box. That is expected: it only defines functions. pytest is the program that calls them. It looks for:

  • files named test_*.py (or *_test.py),
  • functions inside them whose names start with test,
  • and inside each test, a plain assert. If the condition is true the test passes; if it is false, the test fails and pytest reports the values.

There is no magic in that. Here is the core of what pytest does, written out by hand with one test that is wrong on purpose:

The loop walks through every name in the file, calls the ones that start with test_, and treats an AssertionError as a failure. pytest adds a lot on top (good reports, finding files, fixtures), but this is the idea.

#Step 5: Run it, then break it

In the terminal, run:

Each . is one passing test. The first lines vary by computer; the last line is the verdict. Now change 70 to 60 in the first test, save, and run python -m pytest again:

Read the E lines first. assert 70 == 60 shows what was compared, and where 70 = withdraw(100, 30) shows where the 70 came from. Here the test is wrong, not the function, so fix the test back to 70. Sometimes it is the other way round, and deciding which one is wrong is a skill you will practise all course. Add -v (python -m pytest -v) any time you want one line per test with its name and PASSED or FAILED.

#Step 6: Run tests from the Testing view

VS Code can run the same tests with a click. Select the beaker icon in the Activity Bar on the left to open the Testing view. If it shows Configure Python Tests, select it, choose pytest, and pick the root folder (.). Your two tests appear in a tree; the play button at the top runs them all, and each gets a green tick or a red cross. A small play icon also appears next to every test function in the editor.

#When it doesn't work

⚠️ `No module named pytest`

pytest is installed in a different Python from the one running your tests. Check that the prompt shows (.venv) and that VS Code's Status Bar shows the .venv interpreter, then run python -m pip install pytest again in that terminal.

⚠️ `error: externally-managed-environment`

On Chromebooks, many Linux systems, and Homebrew Pythons, pip refuses to install into the system Python. That refusal is protecting you: it means the environment isn't active. Activate .venv (Step 2) and run the install again.

⚠️ Windows: "Activate.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system"

PowerShell blocks scripts by default. Run this once, then try activating again:

⚠️ `collected 0 items` and `no tests ran`

pytest found no tests. Either the file name doesn't start with test_ (for example bank_checks.py), a function name doesn't start with test, or the file isn't saved yet. Rename, save, and run again.

#Two good videos

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You run pip install pytest in a terminal without (.venv), then run tests in VS Code with the .venv interpreter. What happens?

  • It is installed, but only into the Python that pip belonged to, not into .venv.

  • Each environment only sees its own packages, so .venv still has no pytest.

  • VS Code may offer to, but nothing installs without you choosing to.

Show answer

B. Each environment only sees its own packages, so .venv still has no pytest.

2Which of these will pytest collect and run by default?

  • The file name is right, but the function must start with test.

  • Only .py files named test_*.py or *_test.py are searched.

  • Both the file and the function follow pytest's naming rules.

Show answer

C. Both the file and the function follow pytest's naming rules.

3A test fails with E assert 70 == 60 and where 70 = withdraw(100, 30). What do you know for sure?

  • The report shows both sides of the comparison and where the left side came from.

  • Maybe, maybe not. Here 70 is correct, so the test itself is wrong.

Show answer

A. The report shows both sides of the comparison and where the left side came from.

Key takeaways

  • A virtual environment is a per-project Python with its own packages. Create it with python -m venv .venv and select it in VS Code.
  • Use python -m pip and python -m pytest so both use the environment's Python.
  • pytest runs functions named test... in files named test_*.py, and a failing assert becomes a readable report.
  • Read the E lines of a failure first, then decide whether the code or the test is wrong.

#Further reading

  • venv: creation of virtual environments (opens in a new tab): the official reference, including the activation command for every shell.
  • pytest: get started (opens in a new tab): install, first test, and grouping tests, in about ten minutes of reading.
  • Python testing in VS Code (opens in a new tab): everything the Testing view can do, including debugging a single test.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Lay out your oop-python folder so every module's code and tests are easy to find.
  • Split a file into code (bank.py) and tests (test_bank.py) and run them with pytest.
  • Know how the code cells on these pages relate to the files on your computer.
  • Read a traceback from the bottom up and use the debugger to watch values change.
  • Follow a short routine when nothing works.

By the end of this course your project folder will hold dozens of files, and some of them will be broken at any given moment. That is normal. What separates a calm programmer from a frustrated one is mostly habits: where files live, how code and tests are split, and what to do in the first ten minutes after something breaks.

#One folder per module

Make one folder for each module inside oop-python. The virtual environment stays at the top, shared by everything.

Drag check_setup.py and where_am_i.py from the last two lessons into m1_setup in the Explorer, so the top level stays clean. (test_first.py gets replaced in the next section.) Then run tests from inside the folder you are working on:

Why not run everything from the top? If two folders each have a test_bank.py, pytest refuses with an import file mismatch error, because Python can only hold one module called test_bank at a time. Working inside one folder avoids that, and keeps each test run fast and focused.

#Split the code from its tests

Last lesson, withdraw and its tests lived in one file. Real projects keep them apart: the code goes in a module, and the tests import it. Make m1_setup/bank.py holding withdraw plus one new function, apply_all, which adds a list of amounts to a balance. Make m1_setup/test_bank.py holding the two old tests plus one for apply_all, then delete test_first.py. The test file starts with one new line, from bank import apply_all, withdraw. (The block further down shows both files' contents together.)

With both files saved, python -m pytest -v inside m1_setup prints:

#How the code on these pages relates to your files

Every code block on this site with an Output box was really run when the page was built; nobody typed that output. Each block is its own little program, though, so a page can't import one block from another. When a lesson tests something, it puts the code and its tests in one block and ends with a few lines that call the tests, just like tiny_runner.py did:

When you copy a block like this into your project, split it in two: everything above the tests goes in the code file, the tests go in the test file (with the from ... import line at the top), and you drop the loop at the bottom, because pytest does that job for you.

💡 Save before you test

pytest reads the file on disk, not what is on your screen. A dot on the editor tab means unsaved changes. Turn on File › Auto Save and this stops being a problem.

#Read a traceback from the bottom up

Here is a bug. One amount arrived as text, maybe from a form or a file:

Start at the last line: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'. That is what went wrong: Python was asked to add a number and a string. Then read upward for where: each File ..., line ..., in ... entry is one function call, with the most recent call at the bottom. Here the crash happened on line 3 inside apply_all, which was called from line 7. The fix belongs wherever the bad value came in, which might not be the line that crashed.

Most bugs in this course end in one of a few error types. AttributeError means an object has no attribute with that name (often a typo, and Python usually suggests the right one). TypeError usually means the wrong number or kind of arguments. NameError means a name was never defined in that scope.

#Watch values change, one line at a time

A traceback tells you where a program died. To see how it got there, step through it. Press Next below and watch balance change inside apply_all, while start stays put in the outer frame:

Notice that apply_all gets its own box on the call stack while it runs, with its own balance. Changing that balance never touches start. These step-through players appear throughout the course, especially once objects start changing.

VS Code's debugger does the same thing for your real files:

  1. Click in the gutter to the left of a line number (or press F9) to set a breakpoint, shown as a red dot.
  2. Press F5. If VS Code asks which debugger or configuration to use, choose Python Debugger, then Python File.
  3. The program stops on your breakpoint. The Variables pane on the left shows every local variable, and you can expand objects to see inside them.
  4. Press F10 to step over a line, F11 to step into a function call, and F5 to continue.

#A routine for when you're stuck

Two habits make the biggest difference. First, shrink the problem: copy the failing part into a new file and delete everything that isn't needed for the bug to happen. Often the bug becomes obvious halfway through. Second, when you do ask someone, include the code, the complete error, and what you expected to happen. "It doesn't work" gives a helper nothing to go on.

For exploring, two built-in helpers are worth remembering. dir(something) lists every attribute and method it has, and help(something) prints its documentation. Try help(str.split) in the Python REPL (Python: Start Terminal REPL in the Command Palette).

Check your understanding

2 questions

1A traceback ends with AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'push'. Where should you look first?

  • The final line says what went wrong. Python lists use append, not push.

  • The top of a traceback is the oldest call. The cause is described at the bottom.

  • The error is about calling a method that lists don't have, wherever that call is.

Show answer

A. The final line says what went wrong. Python lists use append, not push.

2You edit bank.py, run python -m pytest, and the old failure appears again unchanged. What is the most likely reason?

  • pytest reruns your tests every time.

  • pytest reads files from disk. Save (or turn on Auto Save) and run again.

  • A broken environment gives import errors, not an identical old failure.

Show answer

B. pytest reads files from disk. Save (or turn on Auto Save) and run again.

Key takeaways

  • Keep one folder per module, and run python -m pytest from inside the folder you're working on.
  • Code goes in bank.py; tests go in test_bank.py and import from it. On these pages, both sit in one block with a short loop that calls the tests.
  • Read tracebacks bottom-up: the last line says what, the lines above say where.
  • Breakpoints and stepping show you how values change; use them when a traceback isn't enough.

#Further reading

  • Debugging Python in VS Code (opens in a new tab): breakpoints, configurations, and the debug console in full.
  • Errors and exceptions (opens in a new tab): the Python tutorial's chapter on reading and handling errors.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why data that belongs together breaks when it is kept in parallel lists.
  • Write a class with __init__, attributes, and methods, and create several instances of it.
  • Say exactly what self is when a method runs.
  • Predict how an object's state changes as methods are called, including when two names share one object.

A tiny bank keeps its records in two lists. Ben closes his account, so the program removes his name. A minute later, Cho checks her balance:

Cho had 300 dollars. The program says she has 45, which was Ben's. Nothing crashed and no error appeared, which makes this the worst kind of bug.

#Data that belongs together should travel together

In that script, the only thing connecting "Cho" to 300 is that they sit at the same position in two different lists. Every line of code that adds, removes, or sorts accounts has to update both lists in exactly the same way, forever. One forgotten line and the lists drift apart.

The fix is to stop splitting a single account across several containers. An account is one thing with a name and a balance, so it should be one value in the program. A dict like {"owner": "Cho", "balance": 300} gets part of the way. A class goes further: it bundles the data with the operations that are allowed on it, so the rules ("no overdrafts") live in one place instead of being repeated by every caller.

#A class describes a kind of thing; an instance is one of them

Here's the intuition. A class is like a blank form for opening an account: it says which boxes exist. Each filled-in form is an instance, a separate object with its own values in those boxes. Now precisely:

What happened, line by line:

  • class Account: defines a new type. Nothing is created yet.
  • Account("Ana", 120) creates a new, empty object and then automatically calls __init__ on it with "Ana" and 120. Inside __init__, self is that new object.
  • self.owner = owner creates an attribute: a variable that belongs to that one object. ana.owner and cho.owner are different attributes on different objects.
  • vars(cho) shows the attributes stored on cho, as a dict. Under the hood, an object's attributes really are kept in a dict like that.

#Methods are functions that receive the object as self

A method is a function defined inside a class. You call it on an instance with a dot, and Python quietly passes the instance in as the first argument.

The second call is the key to the whole idea. ana.deposit(30) is shorthand for Account.deposit(ana, 30): look up deposit on the class, then call it with ana as the first argument. That first parameter is named self by convention. It isn't a keyword, just the name every Python programmer uses, so always use it.

Diagrams like this one are class diagrams. The top half lists the attributes each instance carries; the bottom half lists the methods. You will draw one before writing most classes in this course, because it forces you to decide what an object knows and what it can do.

#State changes over time, one method call at a time

An object's state is the current value of all its attributes. Methods are how state changes. This version adds a withdraw that refuses to overdraw and returns whether it worked. Before stepping through, predict the final values of ana.balance and ok.

Three things to notice as you step:

  1. Each method call gets its own frame on the call stack, holding self and the arguments. The frame disappears when the method returns.
  2. When deposit changes self.balance, the global ana changes in the same step. They are not copies; self and ana are two names for one object.
  3. The failed withdraw(80) leaves the balance at 50. The object refused to enter a bad state, and no caller had to remember the rule.

#Two names can point at one object

Assignment never copies an object. It makes another name for the same one:

joint.deposit(25) changed ana.balance because there is only one object. is asks "same object?", so ana is joint is True. twin holds identical data but is a separate object, so ana is twin is False. And ana == twin is also False: by default, == on your own classes falls back to is. Module 4 shows how to teach a class what "equal" should mean.

Now the opening bug, fixed. Each account is one object, so removing Ben removes his whole record at once:

#The classic mistakes

⚠️ Forgetting self in the parameter list

If you write def deposit(amount):, Python still passes the object in first, so there is one argument too many:

The message "takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given" almost always means a missing self. Add it as the first parameter.

⚠️ Forgetting self. inside a method

balance = balance + amount (without self.) talks about a local variable named balance, which doesn't exist yet. Python raises UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'balance' where it is not associated with a value. Attributes are always reached through self..

⚠️ Forgetting the parentheses

print(ana.describe) prints something like <bound method Account.describe of <__main__.Account object at 0x10f3...>>. That's the method itself, not its result. Call it: ana.describe().

#See it explained another way

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this print? a = Account("Ana", 10), then b = a, then b.deposit(5), then print(a.balance, b.balance)

  • That would need b to be a copy, but assignment only creates a second name.

  • a and b are the same object, so the deposit shows up through both names.

  • The deposit was made through b, and both names see the one object anyway.

Show answer

B. a and b are the same object, so the deposit shows up through both names.

2Inside deposit(self, amount), what is self when you call cho.deposit(40)?

  • No copy is made; changes to self change cho.

  • cho.deposit(40) runs Account.deposit(cho, 40), so self is cho.

  • The class is where the method is found, but self is the instance.

Show answer

B. cho.deposit(40) runs Account.deposit(cho, 40), so self is cho.

3A method has the line balance = self.balance - amount and the balance never changes. What's the bug?

  • The new value is stored in a local that vanishes when the method returns. Write self.balance = ....

  • Reading self.balance is fine; the problem is where the result is stored.

  • They can and should; that's how state changes.

Show answer

A. The new value is stored in a local that vanishes when the method returns. Write self.balance = ....

4Why does a list of Account objects avoid the parallel-list bug?

  • They aren't, and sorting isn't the issue.

  • Removing, sorting, or filtering moves whole accounts, never half of one.

  • Memory has nothing to do with the bug.

Show answer

B. Removing, sorting, or filtering moves whole accounts, never half of one.

Key takeaways

  • A class defines a kind of thing; calling it (Account("Ana", 120)) creates an instance and runs __init__ on it.
  • Attributes (self.balance) belong to one instance. Methods are functions that receive that instance as self.
  • obj.method(x) means Class.method(obj, x). That is all self is.
  • Assignment shares an object rather than copying it; is tells you whether two names point at the same one.

What you'll learn

  • Replace three parallel lists with one class whose instances own their data.
  • Write methods that validate input and refuse changes that would break the object's rules.
  • Keep a per-object history and turn it into a readable statement.
  • Make two objects cooperate in a transfer without ever creating or losing money.
  • Protect the behaviour with pytest tests.

Here is where we're headed. By the end of this page, these six lines print two bank statements, and five tests guard every rule behind them:

Make a folder m2_objects in your project, and inside it a file called account.py. Each step below adds to that file.

#Step 1: Look at what we're replacing

This is a typical "before" script. It works, but look at what every function needs: an index i into three lists that must stay perfectly in line.

Adding a fourth piece of data (say, an account type) means a fourth list and edits to every function. Anyone can also write balances[0] = -500 and nothing stops them.

#Step 2: One object per account

Start account.py with a class whose __init__ sets up the three pieces of state. Every new account starts empty, with its own history list.

Adding to ana.history doesn't touch ben.history, because __init__ runs once per account and makes a fresh [] each time. Keep that in mind; module 3 shows a sneaky way to accidentally share one list between every account.

#Step 3: Deposits and withdrawals that enforce the rules

Now the methods. Each one checks its input first, then changes the balance, then records what happened. If a request is impossible, it raises a ValueError instead of quietly doing nothing.

Each history entry is a tuple: a note, the signed amount, and the balance after the change. Storing the running balance means a statement never has to recompute anything. Now try to overdraw:

The program stops with a clear message, and the balance never went negative. A raise ends the method immediately, so the lines that change the balance never run. Module 5 covers catching these errors and making your own error types; for now, a crash with a good message is exactly what we want.

#Step 4: A statement the account prints about itself

Add a statement method. It reads the object's own state and builds a string; it changes nothing.

The format codes line the columns up: <10 pads the note to 10 characters on the left, >+6 right-aligns the amount in 6 characters with a + or - sign, and >4 right-aligns the balance. Returning a string instead of printing makes the method easy to test.

#Step 5: Transfers, and why withdraw raises

A transfer is a withdrawal from one account and a deposit into another. The method takes the other account object as a parameter, so two objects cooperate:

Here is why raising matters. Suppose withdraw returned False on failure, like the version in the Notes lesson, and transfer forgot to check it:

Ben received 500 dollars that never existed. A return value is easy to ignore; an exception is not. With the raising withdraw, the error stops transfer on its first line, so other.deposit never runs. Step through a successful transfer and watch three frames stack up, then watch both objects change:

Inside transfer, self is ana and other is ben. When transfer calls self.withdraw(amount), a new frame opens on top with its own self, which is still ana. When it calls other.deposit(amount), the new frame's self is ben. Same method code, different object.

#Step 6: Lock it in with tests

Make test_account.py next to account.py. On this page the class and tests share one block; in your project, the tests go in their own file starting with import pytest and from account import Account. pytest.raises(ValueError) is a check that passes only if the code inside it raises that error.

The last test is the important one: it proves the "free money" bug can't come back. In your project, run python -m pytest inside m2_objects:

#The finished account.py

The demo sits under if __name__ == "__main__": so it runs when you press play on account.py, but not when test_account.py imports the class.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does withdraw raise ValueError instead of returning False when there isn't enough money?

  • Speed isn't the reason; the difference is whether the caller can ignore the failure.

  • The exception stops transfer before other.deposit runs, which is what keeps money from appearing.

  • They can; it just makes this particular failure easy to miss.

Show answer

B. The exception stops transfer before other.deposit runs, which is what keeps money from appearing.

2Why does transfer call self.withdraw(...) instead of writing self.balance = self.balance - amount directly?

  • Reusing withdraw means every rule applies to transfers automatically, and fixing a rule fixes it everywhere.

  • They can; withdraw itself does.

  • It is shorter, but the real win is having one place that enforces the rules.

Show answer

A. Reusing withdraw means every rule applies to transfers automatically, and fixing a rule fixes it everywhere.

3Each history entry stores the balance after the change. What does that buy us?

  • Storing the balance doesn't affect undoing.

  • Each line already knows the balance at that moment.

Show answer

B. Each line already knows the balance at that moment.

Key takeaways

  • An object owns its data, so adding a new piece of state is one line in __init__, not a new list threaded through every function.
  • Methods validate first, then change state, then record. If a change is impossible, raise, so nobody can ignore the failure.
  • Methods can take other objects as arguments; inside them, self and other are just two different instances.
  • A test for the failure case (test_failed_transfer_changes_nothing) is what stops an old bug from returning.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a close() method that refuses if the balance isn't zero, and make deposit refuse on a closed account.
  • Add undo_last(), which reverses the most recent deposit or withdrawal using history.
  • Give each account a monthly withdrawal limit and a test that proves it works.

#Further reading

  • pytest: how to write and report assertions (opens in a new tab): the rules behind assert in tests and how pytest.raises works.
  • Format specification mini-language (opens in a new tab): every code like <10 and >+6 used in statement.

A Shelf has copies, and each copy has a book. Objects that hold other objects are the subject of the next module.

#Challenge: Members who borrow, without the records disagreeing

Add a Member(name) class with a loans list. member.borrow(copy) must update both sides: the copy's borrower becomes the member, and the copy is added to member.loans. A member can hold at most 3 loans, and a copy that is already out can't be borrowed. member.give_back(copy) undoes both sides. Write tests for: a normal borrow, the loan limit, borrowing a copy that's already out, and giving back.

The hard part is consistency. If borrow updates the member and then fails on the copy, the two records disagree. Look at how the relationships fit together before you start:

Need a hint?

Do every check (limit reached? copy already out?) before changing anything. Only when all checks pass, change both sides. That's the same "validate, then change" order the Account used.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what happens, in order, when you call a class, and validate input in __init__.
  • Use default arguments in constructors without sharing one list between every object.
  • Tell class attributes from instance attributes and predict which one a lookup finds.
  • Extend a class with inheritance and super(), and know when to use composition instead.

Predict what this prints before you look at the output. Ana makes a deposit; we print Ben's history.

Ben's history contains Ana's deposit, and the second line shows why: both accounts hold the same list. Nothing in the code looks shared. The bug comes from how defaults work, and fixing it starts with knowing exactly what a constructor does.

#What happens when you call a class

Account("Ana") does two things. First Python creates a new, empty object of that class. Then it calls __init__ on that object with your arguments, and hands the object back to you. __init__ doesn't create the object, it initializes it, which is why it must not return anything.

That makes __init__ the one place every object passes through, so it is the right place to refuse bad input. If the constructor raises, the caller never gets an invalid object at all:

The first account is created and its name tidied. The second never exists.

#Defaults are evaluated once

A default value is created once, when Python runs the def line, not each time the function is called. For numbers and strings that doesn't matter, since you can't change them in place. For a list, every call that uses the default gets that one list, so every account appends to it.

The fix is to use None as the default and make a fresh list inside the method:

list(history) also copies any list a caller passes in, so the account can't be changed behind its back by someone still holding the original.

#Class attributes are shared by every instance

Attributes assigned on self belong to one instance. Attributes written directly in the class body belong to the class, and every instance can read them. That suits values that are the same for everyone, like an interest rate, or a counter for handing out account numbers.

When you read ana.rate, Python looks on ana first, and if it isn't there, on the class. Step through this and watch what ben.rate = 0.05 really does:

When ben.rate = 0.05 runs, ben gains its own rate attribute (it appears in his box), which hides the class value for Ben only. The class still says 0.02, and so does Ana. Assigning through an instance never changes the class. That is also why __init__ writes Account.next_number += 1: writing self.next_number += 1 would read the class's 1, then store 2 on that one instance, and every account would get number 1.

#Inheritance: a SavingsAccount is an Account

Sometimes a new class is a more specific version of an existing one. A savings account is an account: it has an owner and a balance and can be withdrawn from, but it also earns interest and limits withdrawals. Inheritance says that directly:

class SavingsAccount(Account) means "start with everything Account has". SavingsAccount overrides withdraw with its own version, and inside it, super().withdraw(amount) runs the parent's version, so the overdraft check isn't copied. super().__init__(owner, balance) does the same for setup: the parent sets owner and balance, then the child adds its own attributes.

Step through it and look at the call stack while withdraw runs. There are two withdraw() frames: the savings version underneath, and Account's version on top, called through super(). Both have the same self.

#Composition: a Bank has accounts

Is a bank an account? No. A bank has accounts. That is composition: one object holds others as attributes and uses them. Inheritance is tempting here because it gives you methods for free, so it is worth seeing what goes wrong:

By inheriting from list, Bank picked up all eleven public list methods, including clear, pop, and sort, none of which a bank should offer. With composition, the bank keeps its list private-ish and offers only the operations that make sense:

A good test for inheritance is substitution: could you hand a SavingsAccount to any code that expects an Account and have it still make sense? Yes, so inheritance fits. Could you hand a Bank to code expecting a list? Technically yes, which is exactly the problem. When the honest answer is "has a", use composition.

#Mistakes to watch for

⚠️ Forgetting super().__init__()

If the child's __init__ doesn't call the parent's, the parent's attributes are never set. With SavingsAccount.__init__ setting only self.rate, the first use of the balance fails with AttributeError: 'SavingsAccount' object has no attribute 'balance'. Call super().__init__(...) first.

⚠️ A list, dict, or set as a default argument

def __init__(self, items=[]) shares one list between every object that uses the default. Use items=None and create the list inside.

⚠️ Updating a class attribute through self

self.count += 1 creates an instance attribute and leaves the class's value alone. To change the shared value, write the class name: Account.count += 1.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1def __init__(self, tags=[]) is used to create two objects without passing tags. One object appends "new" to its tags. What do the other object's tags contain?

  • __init__ does run twice, but both runs get the same default list.

  • The default is created when def runs, so every call using it gets the same list.

  • Python allows it, which is what makes the bug easy to write.

Show answer

B. The default is created when def runs, so every call using it gets the same list.

2The class has rate = 0.02. You run a.rate = 0.1. What is Account.rate now?

  • Assigning through an instance creates an attribute on that instance only.

  • That would need Account.rate = 0.1.

  • Assigning a new attribute to an instance is always allowed.

Show answer

A. Assigning through an instance creates an attribute on that instance only.

3A Library needs to store books and look them up by title. Which design fits best?

  • It also gets clear, popitem, and everything else a dict offers, which a library shouldn't expose.

  • A library has books. Composition exposes only the operations that make sense.

  • A book isn't a kind of library, so this inheritance is backwards.

Show answer

B. A library has books. Composition exposes only the operations that make sense.

4Inside SavingsAccount.withdraw, what does super().withdraw(amount) do?

  • There is only one object. super() finds the parent's method, not a parent object.

  • It looks up the next class in line and runs its method on this same savings account.

  • That would recurse forever; super() skips the current class.

Show answer

B. It looks up the next class in line and runs its method on this same savings account.

Key takeaways

  • Calling a class creates an empty object, then __init__ initializes it. Validate there and no invalid object can exist.
  • Defaults are created once. Use None for lists, dicts, and sets, and build a fresh one inside.
  • Reading an attribute checks the instance, then the class. Assigning through an instance only ever changes that instance.
  • Use inheritance for "is a" (and only when a child can stand in anywhere the parent is used), with super() to reuse the parent's code. Use composition for "has a".

  • Python's super() considered super! (opens in a new tab): a core developer's classic article on what super() really does, including with several parents.

What you'll learn

  • Replace tuples with small objects, and see what composition buys in readability.
  • Number accounts automatically with a class attribute and validate them in __init__.
  • Build a Bank that holds accounts and coordinates transfers between them.
  • Add a SavingsAccount with inheritance and super(), and give every account type the same month-end method.

Last module's Account could only stand alone. Real banks have many accounts, of more than one kind, and the bank, not the account, decides how money moves between them. Here is the design we'll build, and the output of its demo:

Make a new folder m3_relationships with a file bank.py. On this page, the code cells share their variables like a notebook, so later steps can use earlier classes.

#Step 1: Transactions become objects

In module 2, each history entry was a tuple like ("deposit", 120, 120). Code that reads it says entry[1], and you have to remember that position 1 means amount. A tiny class gives each piece a name:

An account will have a list of these. That is composition at its smallest: an object built out of other objects, each with one clear job.

#Step 2: Numbered, validated accounts

Each account gets a number from a class attribute that counts upward, and the constructor refuses a blank owner. An opening deposit is optional, and goes through deposit so it is recorded like any other.

Account.next_number is written with the class name on purpose. Every kind of account, including the savings accounts coming in Step 4, should draw from the same counter, so no two accounts ever share a number.

#Step 3: A Bank that holds the accounts

The bank keeps its accounts in a dict keyed by number, so finding one is a single lookup. Notice that transfer finds both accounts before touching any money. If either number is wrong, nothing changes.

Bank doesn't inherit from dict, so callers can't clear() it or pop() an account out from under it. It offers five operations, and every one of them keeps the bank in a valid state. The transfer logic also moved here from Account: deciding which accounts money flows between is the bank's job.

#Step 4: A SavingsAccount that is an Account

A savings account behaves like an account with two extra rules: it allows 3 withdrawals a month and earns interest. It inherits everything else.

super().__init__ gives the savings account its number, owner, balance, and history, using exactly the code from Step 2. The overridden withdraw adds the monthly check and then hands the real work back to Account.withdraw, so the overdraft rule exists in one place only. And because a SavingsAccount is an Account, bank.add(saver) and bank.transfer(...) work with it unchanged.

#Step 5: Month end, without asking "what type are you?"

At the end of each month, savings accounts earn interest and reset their withdrawal count, while ordinary accounts do nothing. The tempting version checks types:

This works today, but every new account type means editing this function, and it reaches inside the account to change its balance without recording a transaction. Instead, give every account a month_end method and let each class decide what that means. Add one method to each of the three classes:

The bank no longer knows or cares which kinds of account it holds. Calling the same method on different kinds of objects and having each respond in its own way is called polymorphism. The interest goes through deposit, so it shows up in the history like any other transaction. You'll see the result in the finished program's output: Ben's interest +11 line.

#Step 6: The finished bank.py

#Step 7: Test the rules that matter

These tests target the decisions we made: one shared counter, the savings limit, month end, and transfers that fail safely. Put them in test_bank.py beginning with import pytest and from bank import Account, Bank, SavingsAccount. Here they run against the classes from the cell above:

In your project, python -m pytest in m3_relationships reports 6 passed.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does Account.__init__ use Account.next_number += 1 rather than self.next_number += 1?

  • It is; __init__ sets several attributes on self.

  • Reading self.next_number finds the class value, but storing it puts the new value on the instance, so the class counter never moves.

  • Any code can change a class attribute through the class name.

Show answer

B. Reading self.next_number finds the class value, but storing it puts the new value on the instance, so the class counter never moves.

2Why does Bank.month_end call account.month_end() instead of checking isinstance(account, SavingsAccount)?

  • Each class owns its month-end rules, and the bank stays the same as types are added.

  • It does: isinstance(saver, Account) is True.

  • Speed isn't the point; keeping rules in the class that owns them is.

Show answer

A. Each class owns its month-end rules, and the bank stays the same as types are added.

3bank.transfer(1001, 9999, 40) raises because 9999 doesn't exist. Why is Ana's balance still unchanged?

  • It doesn't. Anything changed before the error stays changed.

  • The lookup for 9999 fails on the second line, before withdraw runs.

Show answer

B. The lookup for 9999 fails on the second line, before withdraw runs.

Key takeaways

  • Small objects like Transaction replace "remember what index 1 means" with names.
  • Use a class attribute, updated through the class name, for anything every instance must share, like a number counter.
  • Bank has accounts (composition) and exposes only safe operations. SavingsAccount is an account (inheritance) and reuses its code with super().
  • Give every class the same method and let each implement it its own way; callers then never need to check types.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a CheckingAccount that allows an overdraft of up to $100 by overriding withdraw. Does Bank need any change?
  • Add Bank.statement(number) that prints one account's history in the format from module 2.
  • Charge a $2 fee at month end on ordinary accounts with less than $50, by overriding nothing but Account.month_end.

  • Inheritance in the Python tutorial (opens in a new tab): how method lookup walks from a class to its parents, and what isinstance and issubclass check.
  • Composition over inheritance (opens in a new tab): Brandon Rhodes shows, in Python, how a tangle of subclasses collapses into a few composed objects.

#Exercise 6: Is-a or has-a?

For each pair, decide whether the first should inherit from or hold the second, and write one sentence why. No code needed.

  1. Van and Vehicle
  2. Van and Engine
  3. RoutePlanner and Vehicle

  2. Hold. A van has an engine; a van is not a kind of engine.
  3. Hold. The planner has many vehicles and coordinates them; it can't stand in for one.
  4. Hold. A library has a collection; inheriting would expose clear(), sort(), and every other list method.
  5. It depends, and that's the point. An electric van is a van, but if code assumes every van can do any distance, swapping one in breaks that code. Inheritance only works if the base class lets vehicles say what they can do, for example with a can_reach(km) method. The challenge builds exactly that.

#Challenge: An electric van the planner can trust

Add can_reach(km) to Vehicle (returning True), and an ElectricVan(Van) with a range_km (default 60) that overrides it. Update RoutePlanner.best_for so it only considers vehicles that can carry the load and reach the distance. Then write pytest tests for: a light short trip choosing the bike, a heavy long trip skipping an electric van that can't reach, a trip the electric van wins because it's faster, and a load nobody can carry.

Need a hint?

Make the electric van faster than a normal van (say 45 km/h) so it wins some trips. Its __init__ calls super().__init__(name) and then changes self.speed_kmh and sets self.range_km. In best_for, add and v.can_reach(km) to the filter.

Show solution

The design question from Exercise 6 is answered by can_reach: every vehicle now says whether it can do a trip, so an ElectricVan can stand in for a Van safely. The planner changed by one condition and still contains no type checks.

What you'll learn

  • Mark internal attributes with an underscore and expose them through read-only or validated properties.
  • Write __repr__, __eq__, and __lt__ so objects print, compare, and sort the way you intend.
  • Use @dataclass (with field, frozen, and order) for classes that are mostly data.
  • Add type hints, and explain what they do and don't check.

Here's the bank account from earlier modules, used carelessly. Four lines, four problems:

The class works when used exactly as its author intended. This lesson is about the interface: the part of a class that other code is allowed to touch, and how to make that part hard to misuse.

#An underscore means "not part of the interface"

Python has no private keyword. Instead there is a convention every Python programmer follows: a name starting with one underscore, like _balance, is internal. Code outside the class can technically reach it, but doing so is like reaching behind the counter at a shop: nobody locks you out, and nobody promises it'll still work tomorrow.

Two leading underscores (__pin) trigger name mangling: Python renames the attribute to _Account__pin so a subclass can't accidentally overwrite it. It isn't security, and most code never needs it. A single underscore is the everyday tool.

#@property: an attribute that runs code

Renaming balance to _balance hides it, but callers still need to read the balance. A property gives them a read-only door. It looks like an attribute from outside but runs a method:

Without a setter, assignment fails. The only way to change the balance is through deposit, which checks its input. A property can also have a setter that validates new values. Step through this one and notice that self.owner = owner inside __init__ runs the setter too, so the rule is enforced from the very first moment:

Each assignment to acct.owner opens an owner() frame on the call stack: that's the setter running. The value actually lives in _owner, which is why the object's box shows _owner='Bea'. Because callers write acct.owner either way, you can start with a plain attribute and turn it into a property later without changing any code that uses it.

#Dunder methods plug your class into Python's syntax

Methods with double underscores on both sides ("dunder" methods) are hooks that Python calls for you. print(x) calls x.__str__(), x == y calls x.__eq__(y), sorted(items) uses __lt__, and len(x) calls x.__len__().

  • __repr__ should be unambiguous, ideally looking like code that would rebuild the object. Lists, the debugger, and the REPL all use it. If you also want a friendlier version for print, add __str__.
  • __eq__ decides what "equal" means. Two account objects are the same account when their numbers match. Returning NotImplemented for other types lets Python fall back sensibly, so a == "Ana" is just False.
  • Defining __eq__ switches off the default hashing, so the class can no longer go in sets or be a dict key. __hash__ restores that, using the same field __eq__ compares.

Ordering deserves a moment of design thought. Should accounts sort by number? By balance? There's no single obvious answer, so leave out __lt__ and pass a key when you sort: sorted(accounts, key=lambda a: a.balance). Books on a shelf do have a natural order, author and then title, so __lt__ makes sense there:

#@dataclass writes the boring parts for you

Some classes are mostly data: a transaction, a book record, a point. Writing __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for each is tedious and easy to get subtly wrong. The @dataclass decorator reads the class's annotated fields and generates those methods:

field(default_factory=list) is the dataclass answer to module 3's shared-list bug: it calls list() fresh for every object. frozen=True makes instances read-only after creation, which suits records of things that already happened. order=True would also generate __lt__ and friends, comparing fields in order like tuples.

Use a dataclass when the object is a bundle of values. Keep a regular class, with properties guarding the state, when there are rules to protect, like an account's balance.

#Type hints say what you mean

A type hint writes down what type a variable, parameter, or return value should be. It's documentation the tools can read:

Python stores the hints but does not enforce them when the program runs: deposit("10", "5") happily glues two strings into '105', and the quotes from repr are the only clue it isn't a number. The checking happens in your editor. In VS Code, Pylance underlines calls that don't match the hints; set Python › Analysis: Type Checking Mode to basic in Settings to see more of them. Hints you'll use often: list[str], dict[str, int], tuple[int, ...], and str | None for "a string or nothing".

#Mistakes that bite

⚠️ A property that reads itself

Inside def balance(self), writing return self.balance calls the property again, which calls it again... until RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. The property reads the underscored name: return self._balance.

⚠️ A list as a dataclass default

tags: list[str] = [] fails as soon as the class is defined, with ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field tags is not allowed: use default_factory. Write field(default_factory=list).

⚠️ Defining __eq__ and losing hashing

After adding __eq__, putting an object in a set raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'Account'. Add a __hash__ based on the same fields __eq__ compares, or use @dataclass(frozen=True), which generates both.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1balance is a property with no setter. What does acct.balance = 10 do?

  • Nothing connects the assignment to _balance unless you write a setter that does it.

  • A property without a setter is read-only.

  • Properties live on the class and take priority, so the assignment is refused instead.

Show answer

B. A property without a setter is read-only.

2An Account class defines __eq__ comparing account numbers, but no __hash__. What happens with {acct}?

  • That needs a __hash__, which Python removed when __eq__ was defined.

  • Define __hash__ from the same field (hash(self.number)) to fix it.

  • Sets store the objects themselves, not a field of them.

Show answer

B. Define __hash__ from the same field (hash(self.number)) to fix it.

3With hints def area(w: int, h: int) -> int, what does area("ab", 3) do when the program runs?

  • Python doesn't check hints at runtime.

  • "ab" * 3 is valid Python. Pylance warns you before you run it.

  • Hints never convert values.

Show answer

B. "ab" * 3 is valid Python. Pylance warns you before you run it.

4Which class is the best fit for @dataclass(frozen=True)?

  • It's pure data that should never change, so frozen fits perfectly.

  • Frozen objects can't change, and an account must.

  • The bank's state changes constantly; it needs methods guarding it, not frozen fields.

Show answer

A. It's pure data that should never change, so frozen fits perfectly.

Key takeaways

  • One leading underscore marks internals. @property exposes them read-only, or with a setter that validates.
  • Dunder methods connect your class to print, ==, sorted, len, and friends. Pair __eq__ with __hash__, and only add __lt__ when there's one natural order.
  • @dataclass generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from annotated fields. Use field(default_factory=...) for lists and frozen=True for records that must not change.
  • Type hints document intent and power editor checks, but Python ignores them at runtime.

#Further reading

  • dataclasses in the standard library (opens in a new tab): every option, including field(), frozen, order, and __post_init__ for validation.
  • Special method names (opens in a new tab): the official list of dunder methods and exactly when Python calls each.
  • Type hints cheat sheet (opens in a new tab): the syntax for common hints on one page.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a record class into a frozen dataclass.
  • Hide an object's state behind read-only properties and a validating setter.
  • Check input at the edge of the class, and use type hints so tools catch misuse early.
  • Decide, deliberately, whether a class should define equality.
  • Make a container class work with len(), in, and for.

The module 3 bank works, but only if everyone using it is careful. Anyone can write ana.balance = 1_000_000, append fake entries to ana.history, or deposit the string "20". By the end of this page, every one of those is refused, and the demo prints:

Copy your m3_relationships/bank.py into a new folder, m4_interfaces, and change it step by step. Cells on this page share variables like a notebook.

#Step 1: Transactions become frozen dataclasses

A transaction records something that already happened, so nothing should be able to change it. A frozen dataclass gives us the constructor, a readable repr, equality by value, and immutability, in five lines:

Equality by value is exactly right here: two deposits of 120 that left the balance at 120 are, as records, the same.

#Step 2: State goes behind properties

Each piece of account state gets an underscore, and callers get a property to read it. Only owner has a setter, because renaming an account is allowed, as long as the new name isn't blank. Look at history: it returns a tuple copy, so a caller who tries to append to it gets an error, and the real list stays untouched.

All three attacks bounce off, and the account is unchanged. Inside the class, methods still use self._balance freely. The underscore is a boundary between the class and its callers, not between methods of the same class.

#Step 3: Check amounts at the door, and write down the types

The notes lesson ended with deposit("20") crashing deep inside the method with a confusing message. Two tools fix that, and they work at different times.

Type hints say what you mean, and a type checker reads them before the program runs. Add hints to every method, for example def deposit(self, amount: int, note: str = "deposit") -> None:. Then a file that misuses the class gets flagged without running it. Pylance does this in VS Code as you type; the command-line checker mypy (python -m pip install mypy, then python -m mypy misuse.py) reports the same problems:

A runtime check catches whatever the type checker didn't see, such as a value read from a file. Because both deposit and withdraw need it, it goes in one small helper:

type(amount) is not int is stricter than isinstance, on purpose: True is technically an int in Python, and nobody means to deposit True dollars. The leading underscore on _check_amount says it's a helper for this module, not something callers should use.

#Step 4: A repr for debugging, and a decision about equality

Add a __repr__ to Account, so lists of accounts, the debugger, and error messages show something useful. Using type(self).__name__ means a savings account labels itself correctly without its own __repr__:

Should Account also get an __eq__? Ask what equality would mean. Two accounts with the same owner and balance are still two different accounts; and since the bank hands out unique numbers, no two account objects can share a number. Python's default, where an object is only equal to itself, is already correct. So we deliberately leave __eq__ out. Transaction is the opposite case: it's a value, and the dataclass compares it by value.

#Step 5: The Bank acts like a collection

Callers often want to ask "how many accounts?", "is 1002 here?", and "give me each account". Three dunder methods answer those using the familiar syntax, without exposing the dict itself:

__iter__ hands back an iterator over the accounts, so for account in bank: works, and so do sorted(bank, ...), list(bank), and sum(...) over the bank. month_end and total_held can now loop over self directly. Iterator comes from collections.abc, imported at the top of the file.

#Step 6: The finished bank.py

SavingsAccount.month_end reads self.balance (the property) but changes the balance only through self.deposit, so even a subclass goes through the front door and every change is recorded.

#Step 7: Tests that prove the interface holds

Each test tries to misuse the class and checks that it can't. In your project, test_bank.py starts with from dataclasses import FrozenInstanceError, import pytest, and from bank import Account, Bank, SavingsAccount, Transaction.

python -m pytest in m4_interfaces reports 7 passed. The last test compares a whole Transaction with == in one line, which only reads that cleanly because dataclasses compare by value.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the history property return tuple(self._history) instead of self._history?

  • Memory isn't the reason. The point is who can change the history.

  • Returning the real list would let any caller append fake entries or clear it.

  • They can return anything; returning the internal list just defeats the purpose.

Show answer

B. Returning the real list would let any caller append fake entries or clear it.

2Why does Account deliberately have no __eq__?

  • Equality by value fits values like Transaction; accounts are things with identity.

  • They can; there was just no good meaning for it here.

  • It passes using the default identity comparison, because the list holds those exact objects.

Show answer

A. Equality by value fits values like Transaction; accounts are things with identity.

3A type checker already flags deposit("20"). Why keep the runtime _check_amount too?

  • They're reliable for what they can see; the issue is what they can't see.

  • Hints check your code before it runs; the runtime check guards the data it meets later.

  • Python never requires one; hints are optional and unenforced.

Show answer

B. Hints check your code before it runs; the runtime check guards the data it meets later.

Key takeaways

  • A frozen dataclass is the right shape for a record that must not change; it compares by value for free.
  • Underscored state plus read-only properties means state changes only through methods that validate and record.
  • Type hints let tools catch misuse before running; a small runtime check guards values that arrive while running.
  • Only define __eq__ when equality has a clear meaning. Objects with identity, like accounts, are often best left with the default.
  • __len__, __contains__, and __iter__ let a container class work with len, in, and for without exposing its insides.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add Bank.close(number) that refuses unless the balance is zero, and a test proving a closed account is no longer in the bank.
  • Give Transaction a day: int field first and use @dataclass(frozen=True, order=True) so histories sort by day.
  • Run python -m mypy bank.py on your finished file and fix anything it reports.

#Further reading

  • The property built-in (opens in a new tab): the official reference for getters, setters, and deleters.
  • mypy: getting started (opens in a new tab): installing and running a type checker on your own files.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write properties that compute values or validate new ones.
  • Use dataclass options (field, order, frozen, __post_init__) to say exactly what a class means.
  • Implement dunder methods so a value or a collection works with Python's operators.
  • Use type hints and a type checker to find a bug before it crashes.

These exercises move the patterns from the bank into a library and a shop. Work in a new folder, m4_practice. Several exercises raise errors on purpose; reading those errors is part of the practice.

#Warm-up: plain class or dataclass?

Predict the three lines this prints.

Check your prediction

A plain class compares by identity, so two separate objects are never equal. The dataclass generated an __eq__ that compares fields, and a __repr__ that shows them.

#Exercise 1: A thermostat that guards its target

Write Thermostat(room, target). target is a property whose setter refuses anything outside 10 to 30 degrees with a ValueError. Add a read-only property mode that returns "heating" when the room is colder than the target and "idle" otherwise. Remember the constructor should go through the setter too.

Need a hint?

In __init__, write self.target = target (no underscore) so the setter runs. mode needs only a getter; it computes its answer every time from self.room and self._target.

Show solution

mode is never stored, so it can never be out of date. A computed property is the right tool for any value that follows from other state.

#Exercise 2: Fix the inventory record

This dataclass fails before a single object is created. Fix the error, then add a __post_init__ method (dataclasses call it right after their generated __init__) that raises ValueError if quantity is negative.

Need a hint?

The error message names the fix: field(default_factory=list). __post_init__(self) takes no other arguments; read self.quantity inside it.

Show solution

__post_init__ is where a dataclass checks its rules. Note it only runs at creation; for rules that must hold after every change, use a property instead, as in Exercise 1.

#Exercise 3: Sort the shelf

A library shelves books by author, then title. Write a Book dataclass with order=True so sorted() works with no key. It also has a copies count, which should not affect sorting or equality.

The last line is Book("Herbert", "Dune", copies=3) == Book("Herbert", "Dune", copies=1).

Need a hint?

With order=True, fields are compared in the order they are declared, so declare author before title. field(default=1, compare=False) leaves a field out of both == and <.

Show solution

The field order is the sort order. Moving title above author would quietly change how every shelf sorts, so a comment saying so is worth adding in real code.

#Exercise 4: A Money value object

Prices stored as floats drift (0.1 + 0.2 isn't 0.3). Write a frozen dataclass Money that stores whole cents. Add __add__ so two Money values add up (returning NotImplemented for anything else), and __str__ so it prints as dollars.

Need a hint?

__add__(self, other) should return Money(self.cents + other.cents). For the dollars string, divmod(self.cents, 100) gives dollars and remaining cents; format the cents with :02d. To total a list with sum, give it a starting value: sum(prices, Money(0)).

Show solution

Returning NotImplemented (rather than raising yourself) tells Python "I don't know how to add this", and Python produces the standard TypeError. Because Money is frozen, a + b makes a new value and never changes a.

#Exercise 5: A library that works with len, in, and for

Write a Library that keeps books in a private dict keyed by ISBN. add(isbn, title) refuses a duplicate ISBN with ValueError. Implement __len__, __contains__ (so isbn in library works), and __iter__ that yields titles in alphabetical order.

Need a hint?

__iter__ can simply return iter(sorted(self._books.values())) if the dict maps ISBN to title.

Show solution

Callers never see the dict, so you could later switch to a database without changing any code that uses len, in, or for.

#Exercise 6: Let the type hints find the bug

This lookup works for the first ISBN and crashes on the second. Run it, then explain from the type hints why the crash was predictable, and fix the caller so a missing book prints not found.

Need a hint?

Read the return hint out loud: "a Book or None". Every caller has to handle both. A type checker says the same thing; here is mypy's report on this file:

Show solution

The hint -> Book | None was a promise that some calls return None. The checker flagged both lines, even the one that happened to work, because nothing in the code guaranteed it would. After the if book is None check, the checker knows book is a Book in the else branch and stops complaining.

#Challenge: A tested inventory for the school shop

Build an inventory with two classes. Product is a frozen dataclass with sku, name, and price_cents. Inventory keeps products and stock counts in private dicts and offers:

  • add_product(product), refusing a duplicate SKU;
  • receive(sku, qty) and ship(sku, qty), which refuse unknown SKUs, non-positive quantities, and shipping more than is in stock;
  • a read-only way to ask quantity(sku);
  • low_stock(threshold), returning products at or below the threshold, sorted by name;
  • total_value() in cents;
  • __len__ (number of products) and __contains__ (by SKU).

Write pytest tests for at least: receiving and shipping, refusing to oversell (and nothing changing), the low-stock report's order, total value, and that a Product can't be modified.

Need a hint?

A private _require(sku) helper that raises for unknown SKUs keeps receive, ship, and quantity short. Do every check in ship before you subtract anything.

Show solution

Inventory stores stock separately from Product on purpose: a product's price and name are facts about the product, while the count is a fact about this shop, and it changes constantly. Keeping the changing part in the guarded class and the fixed part in a frozen value is the same split as Account and Transaction.
