m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Follow an exception as it travels up the call stack, and read the traceback it leaves.
  • Use try, except, else, and finally, and know exactly which ones run.
  • Raise built-in and custom exceptions, and translate low-level errors with raise ... from.
  • Organize code into modules and packages, and use if __name__ == "__main__": correctly.

Here is a hotel booking loop that a student shipped to their family's guesthouse. It looks careful: every booking is wrapped in try, so the program never crashes. Run it and read the third line of output.

There is no room 103. rooms[103] raised a KeyError, and except Exception caught it and reported a lie. If someone later mistypes append as apend, the same line will tell every guest their room is taken, and nobody will see the real AttributeError. Not crashing is easy. Failing accurately takes design, and that design is what this lesson builds.

#An exception travels up the call stack until something catches it

When Python hits a problem it can't continue past, it creates an exception object and raises it. The current function stops right there. Python then checks the caller: is this call inside a try with a matching except? If not, that function stops too, and the exception moves up again. If it reaches the top with nobody catching it, the program ends and prints a traceback.

Read a traceback from the bottom up. The last line names the exception type and its message: February has no 30th. The lines above it are the path the exception took, oldest call first: the top of the file called book, which called parse_night, whose call to date.fromisoformat raised. The first booking printed normally because nothing went wrong until the second call.

Now catch it at the top instead. Step through this and watch the call stack: when int("two") fails, both parse_guests and make_booking vanish from the stack at once, and execution lands in the except block.

#try, except, else, finally: who runs when

Each of the four blocks has one job. try holds the code that might fail. except runs only if that code raised a matching exception. else runs only if try finished without an exception. finally runs no matter what, even when another block returns.

Both calls return from inside except or else, yet finally still prints before the value comes back. That makes finally the place for cleanup that must happen: closing a connection, saving a file, releasing a lock. Keep the try block small. Only int(text) can raise the ValueError we're expecting, so it's the only line inside try; the success path goes in else, where a bug can't be mistaken for bad input.

#raise: refuse to continue when a rule is broken

Your own classes should raise exceptions too. A constructor is a good place, because it guards the moment an object comes into existence. If a check-out date comes before the check-in date, the right response is to refuse to build the object at all.

Every Stay that exists is now valid, so no other method has to re-check the dates. A useful rule of thumb: raise where you detect the problem, catch where you know what to do about it. Stay can detect a backwards date but can't decide whether to re-prompt a user, log it, or reject a web request. Its caller can.

#Custom exception classes give each failure a name

ValueError says "a value was wrong", but a booking app fails in several distinct ways, and callers need to tell them apart without reading message strings. The fix is a small family of exception classes. They're ordinary classes that inherit from Exception, often with no body beyond a docstring.

Three details matter here. RoomUnavailable stores room and night as attributes, so the handler can use them instead of parsing text. raise InvalidDates(...) from err translates a low-level ValueError into the app's own vocabulary while keeping the original attached as err.__cause__, so a traceback would show both. And Python checks except clauses top to bottom, taking the first match, so the specific class goes before its base class.

⚠️ Watch out

Catching too much. A bare except: or except Exception: around a big block catches your typos too (NameError, AttributeError), as the guesthouse loop showed. Catch the narrowest class you can actually handle, like except BookingError:, and let everything else crash loudly during development. A crash with a traceback is a bug report; a wrong message is a mystery.

⚠️ Watch out

Base class first. If except BookingError comes before except RoomUnavailable, the second clause can never run, because every RoomUnavailable is already a BookingError. Python won't warn you. Order handlers from most specific to most general.

#Modules, packages, and the __main__ guard

As the app grows, one file gets hard to navigate. A module is just a .py file; import runs that file once and gives you access to the names it defined. A package is a folder of modules with an __init__.py file. A booking app might be laid out like this:

Inside models.py you'd write from booking.errors import InvalidDates, RoomUnavailable. Giving the exceptions their own module pays off: every other module can import them, and errors.py imports nothing from the app, so it can never be part of a circular import.

Every module has a variable called __name__. When you run a file directly, Python sets it to "__main__". When the file is imported, __name__ is the module's own name. That's what the familiar guard checks. This cell writes two tiny files and runs each one with the same Python interpreter, the way you would in VS Code's terminal:

Run directly, greet.py sees "__main__" and runs its demo. Imported by app.py, it sees "greet", so the guarded block is skipped. Put the code that starts your program under the guard, and importing the module (from tests, for example) won't launch a menu or print anything.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't shadow the standard library. Name your file random.py or json.py and import random will import your file instead of Python's, giving errors like AttributeError: module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'. Pick specific names like dice.py.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1book() raises RoomUnavailable. The handlers are except BookingError: (prints "A") and then except RoomUnavailable: (prints "B"). What prints?

  • Python takes the first matching clause. RoomUnavailable is a BookingError, so the first clause wins and "B" is unreachable.

  • That needs the specific clause listed first. Order matters.

  • At most one except clause runs per exception.

Show answer

A. Python takes the first matching clause. RoomUnavailable is a BookingError, so the first clause wins and "B" is unreachable.

2What does this function return, and what does it print? try: return "try" followed by finally: print("cleanup")

  • finally runs even when try returns, so "cleanup" is printed.

  • The return value is set aside, finally runs, then the function returns.

  • finally doesn't discard the return value unless it has its own return.

Show answer

B. The return value is set aside, finally runs, then the function returns.

3Hotel.book() detects that a room is taken. Where should the except RoomUnavailable that prints "please pick another room" live?

  • Then book() would have to know about printing and menus, and a web version or a test couldn't react differently.

  • The menu knows how to talk to the user. book() detects the problem and raises; the caller decides what to do.

  • Printing hides the failure from the caller, which then carries on as if the booking worked.

Show answer

B. The menu knows how to talk to the user. book() detects the problem and raises; the caller decides what to do.

4booking/models.py is imported by booking/__main__.py, and you run python -m booking. What is __name__ inside models.py?

  • Only the module Python was asked to run gets that name; here that's booking/__main__.py.

  • An imported module's __name__ is its full dotted import name.

  • __name__ holds the import name, not the file name.

Show answer

B. An imported module's __name__ is its full dotted import name.

Key takeaways

  • An exception climbs the call stack until an except matches it; a traceback is that path, read bottom-up.
  • Keep try blocks tiny, catch the narrowest exception you can handle, and use finally for cleanup that must happen.
  • Raise where you detect a problem; catch where you know what to do about it.
  • A base exception like BookingError, with specific subclasses carrying useful attributes, lets callers handle failures by kind.
  • raise NewError(...) from err translates low-level errors without losing the original.
  • Modules are files, packages are folders with __init__.py, and if __name__ == "__main__": keeps start-up code from running on import.

What you'll learn

  • Lay out a Python package with __init__.py, separate modules, and a __main__.py entry point.
  • Design an exception hierarchy where each class has one clear meaning.
  • Translate low-level errors (ValueError, JSONDecodeError) into your own with raise ... from.
  • Catch errors at the boundary of the program, and use finally so data is always saved.

By the end of this build you'll have a small hotel booking program that you start with python -m booking. It books rooms, refuses double bookings, rejects nonsense dates, survives a damaged save file, and always saves on the way out. Each failure has its own exception class, and only one place in the whole program decides what to print about them.

Here is the folder you'll create, and the path an error takes when someone tries to book a taken room:

Every code cell below is one file of the package, and the cells share their names like a notebook. In a real project the files find each other through import lines; each step tells you exactly which lines to put at the top of the file.

#Step 1: Create the package in VS Code

Open an empty folder called hotel in VS Code (File › Open Folder…). In the Explorer, use the New Folder… button to make booking, then the New File… button to add the five files from the tree above, all inside booking. Put a one-line docstring in __init__.py:

Python treats a folder with an __init__.py as a regular package. The file can stay this short. Later you can re-export names from it, like from booking.models import Hotel, so that users can write from booking import Hotel.

#Step 2: Name every failure in errors.py

Start with the vocabulary of things that can go wrong. Write the hierarchy before any logic, so each later function can say exactly which failure it means.

This file defines classes and prints nothing, so the cell has no output. Poke at it to check that the family tree is what you meant:

RoomUnavailable keeps a description of the clashing stay as a plain string rather than a Stay object. That's deliberate: errors.py stays free of imports from the rest of the app, so any module can import it without creating a loop.

#Step 3: Raise from the models

models.py holds the rules. Its first line in the real file is from booking.errors import InvalidDates, RoomUnavailable, UnknownRoom; in this notebook those names already exist.

Notice what's missing: there isn't a single print or except BookingError in this module. parse_date translates Python's ValueError into the app's InvalidDates, Stay refuses backwards dates, and Hotel.book refuses overlaps. The overlap test uses <, not <=, so a guest can check in on the morning another checks out. Try four bookings, catching only BookingError so you can see which class each failure is:

#Step 4: Save and load without losing the cause

storage.py starts with from booking.errors import StorageError and from booking.models import Hotel, Stay, parse_date. A missing file is normal on the very first run, so load handles it by returning an empty hotel. A damaged file isn't normal, so it becomes a StorageError with the JSON error attached as its cause.

Test all three situations: a round trip, a missing file, and a file someone half-edited by hand.

Because of from err, the original JSONDecodeError rides along as __cause__. If this error ever reached the top of the program uncaught, the traceback would show both, with the line "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" between them.

#Step 5: Catch at the boundary in main.py

The menu imports BookingError from booking.errors, Hotel, Stay, and parse_date from booking.models, and load and save from booking.storage. It's the one place that turns exceptions into messages.

Two try blocks, two jobs. The inner one wraps a single command, so one bad booking prints a message and the loop carries on. The outer one has no except at all, only finally: whether the user types quit, presses Ctrl+C (a KeyboardInterrupt, which except BookingError deliberately doesn't catch), or a bug crashes the loop, the bookings are saved first.

#Step 6: Run it as a package

In VS Code's terminal, make sure you're in the hotel folder (the one that contains booking), then run:

-m booking tells Python to find the package called booking and run its __main__.py. Python puts the current folder on its import path, which is why from booking.errors import BookingError works inside the package. Run it a second time and list 201 still shows Eli's stay, because load read it back from bookings.json.

⚠️ Watch out

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'booking'. You'll see this if you run python booking/__main__.py instead of python -m booking, or run python -m booking from inside the booking folder. In both cases the folder that contains booking isn't on the import path. Go up to hotel and use -m.

#The finished package

File Starts with Holds
booking/__init__.py (a docstring) marks the package
booking/errors.py no imports BookingError and its four subclasses
booking/models.py from datetime import date, from booking.errors import InvalidDates, RoomUnavailable, UnknownRoom parse_date, Stay, Hotel
booking/storage.py import json, from pathlib import Path, from booking.errors import StorageError, from booking.models import Hotel, Stay, parse_date save, load
booking/__main__.py from pathlib import Path, plus the imports listed in Step 5 handle, main, and the __main__ guard

The imports only point one way: __main__ → storage → models → errors. Keeping that direction is what stops circular imports as the package grows.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does load turn json.JSONDecodeError into StorageError instead of letting it escape?

  • It can; load catches it right there.

  • Callers deal with the package's own vocabulary, and from err still keeps the JSON details for debugging.

  • Nothing repairs the file; the error just gets a clearer name.

Show answer

B. Callers deal with the package's own vocabulary, and from err still keeps the JSON details for debugging.

2A typo in handle calls hotel.bok(room, stay). What happens when someone books a room?

  • That would happen only if the menu caught Exception. It catches BookingError, and an AttributeError isn't one.

  • The bug surfaces immediately with a line number, and the data is still saved on the way out.

  • Misspelled attribute names are only noticed when that line actually runs.

Show answer

B. The bug surfaces immediately with a line number, and the data is still saved on the way out.

3Why is save(hotel, path) in a finally block rather than after the loop?

  • Speed is the same; what changes is when it's guaranteed to run.

  • finally runs on every way out of the try: normal exit, break, or an exception.

Show answer

B. finally runs on every way out of the try: normal exit, break, or an exception.

Key takeaways

  • Put exceptions in their own import-free module so every other module can use them.
  • Models raise specific errors and print nothing; only the boundary (the menu) turns errors into messages.
  • Translate errors from other libraries into your own with raise ... from err so callers learn one vocabulary.
  • A loop-level try/except keeps one bad command from ending the session; an outer finally guarantees cleanup.
  • Run packages from the folder that contains them with python -m package_name.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add cancel ROOM GUEST with a new BookingNotFound exception. Decide where in the hierarchy it belongs.
  • Give UnknownRoom a list of real room numbers and print them in the message.
  • Make save write to bookings.json.tmp first and rename it, so a crash mid-write can't destroy the old file.

  • Packages (opens in a new tab) in the official tutorial covers __init__.py and both absolute and relative imports.

What you'll learn

  • Narrow a catch-all except and find the bug it was hiding.
  • Write constructors and methods that raise precise, informative exceptions.
  • Translate and re-raise exceptions without losing the original cause.
  • Keep a module's demo code from running when it is imported.

Work in a new folder in VS Code, one file per exercise. Type the code yourself instead of pasting it, and run each version before you open the solution. Several of these exercises start with code that misbehaves on purpose.

#Warm-up: predict the letters

Before you look at the output, write down which letters this prints and in what order.

int("x") raises ValueError, so "B" is skipped. The inner handler only catches KeyError, so "C" is skipped too. finally prints "D" on the way out, return value never runs, and the exception climbs to the outer try, which prints "E".

#Exercise 1: Find the bug the catch-all was hiding

This function is supposed to average quiz scores and skip lines that aren't numbers. Run it.

Every line gets "skipped", including "90", and then the program crashes dividing by zero. Change the handler so it catches only the error that bad input causes, put just the risky call inside try, and fix the bug that the narrower handler reveals. Expected output:

Need a hint?

After you switch to except ValueError:, run it again before fixing anything. The traceback now names the real problem and the exact line.

Show solution

With except ValueError, the typo shows up as AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'apend'. Only int(line) is inside try, and the append moved to else, so a future typo there can't be mistaken for bad input.

#Exercise 2: Refuse to build an invalid seat

A theater has rows A to J and seats 1 to 20. This starter accepts any seat at all. Make the constructor raise ValueError with a message that says what was wrong.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

row in "ABCDEFGHIJ" looks like enough, but try "" in "ABCDEFGHIJ" in the terminal. An empty string is found inside every string.

Show solution

The len(row) != 1 check runs first, so both "" and "AB" are rejected before the membership test can be fooled. Using !r in the message puts quotes around the value, which makes an empty string visible.

#Exercise 3: An exception family for library loans

A library lets each member borrow at most 2 books, and a book can only be out to one person at a time. Write LibraryError and two subclasses: NotAvailable, which stores title and due_back, and LimitReached, which stores limit. Then make borrow raise them, so the starter's loop prints the output below.

Need a hint?

Each subclass needs its own __init__ that calls super().__init__(message) and then saves its attributes. In borrow, check availability first, then count how many loans already belong to that member.

Show solution

The handler for NotAvailable reads err.title directly, which is why the attribute exists. LimitReached falls through to the general LibraryError handler, so a third kind of loan error added later would still be handled.

#Exercise 4: Translate errors with raise from

Write load_settings(text) that parses a JSON string and returns the dict. It must raise one custom SettingsError for every way the input can be bad: invalid JSON, a missing "volume" key, or a volume that isn't a whole number from 0 to 10. When the cause was another exception, chain it with from. The starter below crashes on the second string with an uncaught JSONDecodeError:

Expected output once it works:

Need a hint?

Use one try with two except clauses: json.JSONDecodeError and KeyError. The range check isn't caused by another exception, so it uses a plain raise.

Show solution

Callers only ever need except SettingsError, yet __cause__ still tells a developer which low-level failure started it.

#Exercise 5: Retry, then give up honestly

FlakyService.fetch() fails with ConnectionError a set number of times before it works. Write fetch_with_retries(service, attempts=3) that tries up to attempts times, prints each failure, returns the result as soon as one call works, and re-raises the last ConnectionError if every attempt fails.

Calling it with FlakyService(failures=2) and then with FlakyService(failures=5) should print:

Need a hint?

return inside try exits the loop and the function on success. Inside the except block, a bare raise with nothing after it re-raises the exception being handled, traceback and all.

Show solution

Only ConnectionError is retried; any other exception, such as a bug inside fetch, escapes on the first attempt, which is what you want. The last line of the function only runs if attempts is 0 or less, so the loop never ran.

#Exercise 6: Stop a module from talking when imported

grades.py has a handy letter() function and a quick self-test at the bottom. report.py imports it. This cell creates both files and runs report.py:

The self-test line leaks into the report. Rewrite grades.py so its self-test is in a main() function that runs only when grades.py is run directly. python report.py should print just Mia: B, and python grades.py should still print the self-test.

Need a hint?

Importing a module runs every top-level line in it. Move the print into def main(): and call main() under if __name__ == "__main__":.

Show solution

When report.py imports grades, the module's __name__ is "grades", so main() is skipped. Run directly, it's "__main__" and the self-test prints. Wrapping the start-up code in main() also keeps its variables out of the module's global names.

#Challenge: Report every problem at once

A sign-up form that stops at the first mistake is annoying: fix the name, submit, then learn the age was wrong too. Write ValidationError, which stores a list called problems, and validate_signup(form) that checks every field before raising:

  • name must not be blank.
  • age must be digits, and between 13 and 19.
  • email must contain @.

Test it with a good form and with {"name": " ", "age": "fifteen", "email": "rae.example.com"}, printing each problem on its own line.

Need a hint?

Start with problems = [], append a message for each failed check, and raise only once at the end, if problems:. Use elif for the age range so you never call int() on a non-number.

Show solution

One exception carries all the problems, so the caller decides how to show them. Python 3.11 added a built-in version of this idea for exceptions themselves, ExceptionGroup, with a matching except* syntax; read about it in the tutorial's errors chapter once this version makes sense.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain polymorphism and duck typing, and predict which method a call will run.
  • Define an interface with abc.ABC and @abstractmethod, and read the error when a class breaks it.
  • Write unit tests with pytest (assert, pytest.raises, fixtures) and with unittest.
  • Use a fake object to test code that would otherwise send messages or touch files.

Three student projects at one school each needed "do these two date ranges overlap?": the hotel app from last module, a library's loan tracker, and the robotics club's room scheduler. Each project pasted in its own copy. In March someone noticed that a stay ending on the 4th and one starting on the 4th were reported as clashing, and fixed it, in one copy. The other two still had the bug in June.

The cure is one shared component that every project imports. For that to work, the component needs a clear interface (what callers can rely on) and tests (proof that it keeps those promises after every change). This lesson covers both, starting with how Python decides what a method call does.

#Polymorphism: one call, many behaviors

A booking app has to confirm bookings by email for some guests and by text message for others. You could write if channel == "email": ... elif channel == "sms": ... everywhere you send something. Or you could give each channel a class with the same method name, and let the object decide what send means.

Step through this program. Watch the line return channel.send(...) inside confirm: it's the same line both times, but it jumps into a different class's method each time around the loop.

That's polymorphism: code written against one method name works with many classes. confirm will never need editing when you add a Push or Discord class tomorrow.

#Duck typing: Python checks behavior, not ancestry

Notice that Email and Sms don't share a parent class. Python doesn't care. When channel.send(...) runs, Python looks for a send attribute on that particular object, right then. If it has one, the call works. This is duck typing: if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's treated as a duck.

The flip side is that a mistake is only discovered when the call actually happens:

Passing the string "email" instead of an Email object only fails when confirm tries to call .send on it. In a big program, that line might run rarely. That's where an explicit interface helps.

#abc.ABC: write the contract down

The abc module (abstract base classes) lets you declare an interface as a class. Methods marked @abstractmethod have no real body; they're promises. Python refuses to create an object from any class that still has an unkept promise.

Two things happened. EmailNotifier kept the promise, and it also inherited send_all, a normal method written once in the base class that calls whichever send the subclass provides. SmsNotifier misspelled send, and Python stopped it the moment you tried to create one, long before any message needed sending. That's the trade: an ABC moves the error from "whenever this line happens to run" to "as soon as the object is made".

📝 Note

Python also has typing.Protocol, which describes an interface without requiring inheritance. A tool like mypy then checks that any object you pass has the right methods. Use an ABC when you want shared methods like send_all and a runtime check; a Protocol when you just want type checking of duck-typed code.

#Unit tests: one behavior, one test

A unit test is a tiny program that calls one piece of your code and checks one result. You met pytest in Module 1: files named test_*.py, functions named test_*, and plain assert. Here is a test file for the shared overlap function. For a first look, the function and its tests share one file, the way pytest's own getting-started guide does it:

The second test is the March bug, written down forever. pytest.raises passes only if the code inside the with block raises that exception, and match= checks the message too. Test names are sentences, so a failure report reads like a bug report.

Python's standard library has its own testing module, unittest. pytest can run unittest tests too, and since unittest needs no install, it's what runs on this page. The same three tests:

unittest groups tests as methods of a TestCase subclass and uses methods like assertTrue and assertRaises instead of bare assert. In your own files, unittest.main() at the bottom finds and runs the tests for you; the last two lines here do the same thing explicitly.

#Fixtures and fakes: testing code that talks to the world

How do you test confirm_booking without emailing a real person? Because of duck typing, you can pass a fake: an object with the same send method that just records what it was asked to do. And because several tests need a fresh fake, pytest lets you write a fixture, a function marked @pytest.fixture that builds it. Any test that names the fixture as a parameter gets a brand-new copy.

The unittest version of a fixture is a setUp method, which runs before every test method:

test_only_one_message_is_sent passes only because each test gets its own fake. If both tests shared one, the second would see two messages and fail depending on the order the tests ran in. Fresh setup per test is the whole point.

This also shows why interfaces and tests go together. confirm_booking depends on "something with send", not on a real email library, so a fake slots in. Writing a test before the code (test-first) pushes you toward that kind of design, because it's the first moment you have to call your code from outside. You'll work that way in the build-along.

⚠️ Watch out

A test that never runs. pytest only collects functions whose names start with test, in files named test_*.py or *_test.py. Name one check_overlap and pytest silently skips it; unittest likewise ignores methods not starting with test. If the count of tests in the summary is lower than you expected, check the names.

⚠️ Watch out

Fighting duck typing. Code like if isinstance(channel, EmailNotifier): ... elif isinstance(channel, SmsNotifier): ... brings back the if chain polymorphism was meant to remove, and it rejects fakes in tests. Call the method and let each class handle it.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1channels = [EmailNotifier(), FakeNotifier()], and the loop calls channel.send("ana", "hi") on each. FakeNotifier doesn't inherit from Notifier. What happens?

  • Python only looks for a send method on each object when the call runs. Inheritance isn't required.

  • Nothing checks the class at call time; that only happens if you write an isinstance check yourself.

  • Python lists hold any mix of objects.

Show answer

A. Python only looks for a send method on each object when the call runs. Inheritance isn't required.

2PushNotifier(Notifier) defines def push(self, to, text) but no send. When do you first get an error?

  • Defining the class is allowed; it just stays abstract.

  • An ABC blocks creating objects from classes with unimplemented abstract methods.

  • That's how plain duck typing behaves. The ABC moves the error earlier.

Show answer

B. An ABC blocks creating objects from classes with unimplemented abstract methods.

3Two pytest tests both use the notifier fixture. The first test sends one message. How many messages does the second test's notifier start with?

  • A fixture runs again for each test that asks for it, so every test gets a new FakeNotifier.

  • That would happen if the tests shared one object, which is the problem fixtures solve.

  • Fresh fixtures make the order irrelevant.

Show answer

A. A fixture runs again for each test that asks for it, so every test gets a new FakeNotifier.

Key takeaways

  • Polymorphism means one method name, many implementations; callers stay the same when you add a new class.
  • Duck typing checks for the method when it's called; an abc.ABC with @abstractmethod catches a missing method when the object is created.
  • An ABC can also hold shared concrete methods, like send_all, written once for every implementation.
  • A unit test checks one behavior; pytest.raises and assertRaises test that the right exception happens.
  • Fixtures (pytest) and setUp (unittest) give every test fresh objects, so tests can't affect each other.
  • Code that depends on an interface instead of a concrete class can be tested with a fake.

#Further reading

  • Abstract Base Classes (abc) (opens in a new tab), the official reference, including abstract properties and class methods.
  • How to use fixtures (opens in a new tab) in the pytest docs: sharing fixtures across files with conftest.py, and cleanup with yield.
  • The unittest framework (opens in a new tab), for setUp, tearDown, and the full list of assert methods.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Work in red-green-refactor cycles: write a failing test, make it pass, then tidy up.
  • Build a reusable component with a small, clear interface and its own exception.
  • Use setUp in unittest and fixtures plus parametrize in pytest to keep tests short.
  • Reuse one tested component in two different programs.

The overlap bug from the last lesson lived in three copies because three projects each wrote their own date logic. You're going to write that logic once, as a module called dateranges.py, and build it the test-first way: every behavior starts life as a failing test.

Here is the finished component. One class, one exception, five things a caller can do with it:

A range runs from start up to, but not including, end. For a hotel stay, end is the check-out day, so December 1 to December 4 is three nights, and someone else can check in on the 4th. That one rule is where every copy of the old code went wrong, so it gets tested first.

#Step 1: A helper to run tests on this page

In VS Code you'd run python -m pytest (or python -m unittest) in the terminal. On this page, a small helper runs unittest test classes and prints the results. Each cell after this shares names with the ones before it.

#Step 2: Red. Describe nights and bad ranges before they exist

Write down two promises: a range knows how many nights it covers, and it refuses to exist if end isn't after start. DateRange hasn't been written yet, so both tests should fail. Run them anyway.

Two ERRORs with NameError. That's a useful failure: the tests run, and they fail for the reason you expected. A test you've never seen fail might not be testing anything at all.

#Step 3: Green. The simplest class that passes

Both pass. A few design decisions are already baked in. @dataclass(frozen=True) writes __init__, __eq__, and __repr__ for you, and makes the object read-only, so nobody can stretch a booked range after the overlap check approved it. __post_init__ runs right after the generated __init__, which makes it the spot for validation. InvalidRange subclasses ValueError, so older code that already catches ValueError still works, while new code can catch the specific class.

#Step 4: Red, then a bug the tests catch

Next promise: two ranges overlap only if they share a night. These tests use setUp, which builds a fresh stay before each test method.

Now add overlaps. Here it's written the way the robotics club's copy had it, with <=, because "touching" feels like it should count:

Four pass and test_back_to_back_does_not_overlap fails with AssertionError: True is not false. The test caught the exact bug that sat in two projects for three months, and it did it in under a second. The fix is one character in each comparison:

#Step 5: Membership, iteration, and the finished component

Two more promises make the class pleasant to use: day in stay should work, and for day in stay should visit each night. Write the tests first, as always:

Here is the finished dateranges.py, with the overlap fix, the two dunder methods, and a parse class method for text input:

All nine pass. __contains__ uses the same "up to, not including" rule as overlaps, so the two can't disagree. The test for parse compares with ==, which works because the dataclass generated __eq__. This is also the moment for the refactor part of the loop: with nine green tests, you can rename things or restructure the class and know within a second whether you broke a promise.

#Step 6: Reuse it in two projects

The payoff. Here are two unrelated programs, the hotel and the robotics club's room scheduler, both built on the same tested component. In each project, from dateranges import DateRange replaces the old copied logic.

If someone finds another edge case next year, they add a test to test_dateranges.py, fix DateRange once, and both projects get the fix.

#Step 7: The same suite in pytest

Your VS Code project now looks like this:

pytest can run your unittest classes unchanged. Rewritten in pytest style, though, the suite gets shorter: a fixture replaces setUp, and @pytest.mark.parametrize turns a table of cases into separate tests. Save this as test_dateranges.py, and add from dateranges import DateRange, InvalidRange under import pytest (this page already has those names, so the block leaves that line out):

Each row of a parametrize table becomes its own test with its own name, so a failure tells you which case broke. test_overlaps checks both directions on purpose: overlap should be symmetric, and a lopsided implementation would pass a one-way test.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Step 2 the tests were run before DateRange existed. What did that prove?

  • It confirmed something important about the tests themselves.

  • A test that has never failed might be checking nothing, for example if its name doesn't start with test.

  • It can't; that's why the tests errored with NameError.

Show answer

B. A test that has never failed might be checking nothing, for example if its name doesn't start with test.

2Why is InvalidRange a subclass of ValueError instead of Exception?

  • A backwards range really is a bad value, so it fits under ValueError and gains a precise name.

  • __post_init__ can raise anything.

  • Any exception class can take a message.

Show answer

A. A backwards range really is a bad value, so it fits under ValueError and gains a precise name.

3What would frozen=True stop in the hotel project?

  • Equal ranges are allowed; they're just equal.

  • A frozen dataclass raises FrozenInstanceError on assignment, so an approved booking can't be stretched into a clash.

  • __iter__ only reads the fields.

Show answer

B. A frozen dataclass raises FrozenInstanceError on assignment, so an approved booking can't be stretched into a clash.

Key takeaways

  • Red-green-refactor: write the test, watch it fail, write the least code that passes, then tidy while it stays green.
  • The edge case that caused the original bug (back-to-back ranges) should be the first test you write, in both directions.
  • A small frozen dataclass with one clear rule ("up to, not including") makes a good reusable component.
  • setUp in unittest and fixtures in pytest give each test fresh objects; parametrize turns a table of cases into named tests.
  • Fix shared logic once, in one tested module, and every project that imports it gets the fix.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add intersection(other) that returns the shared DateRange, or None if there isn't one. Write the tests first, including back-to-back ranges.
  • Build a second component, ids.py, with a BookingId class that formats IDs like BK-0042 and rejects malformed strings with its own exception.
  • Add a __str__ that prints Dec 1-4, 2026 and test it for ranges that cross a month or a year.

What you'll learn

  • Replace type-checking if/elif chains with classes that share a method name.
  • Define an abc.ABC interface with abstract and shared methods, and implement it twice.
  • Write unittest and pytest tests that expose a bug, and use fakes for clocks and messages.
  • Work from tests to code: read a spec written as tests and make it pass.

These exercises use plain Python and unittest so you can check your answers anywhere; Exercise 6 moves to pytest in VS Code. For each one, write your attempt in its own file before opening the solution.

#Warm-up: whose method runs?

report is defined only in Unit. Predict the three lines before reading the output.

self.label() and self.damage() are looked up on the actual object each time, so Archer swaps in both of its own methods even though report lives in the parent. Knight keeps the inherited label ("unit") and builds its damage on top of the parent's with super().

#Exercise 1: Replace the if/elif chain

Every new shipping option means editing this function, and every caller that checks method == "express" somewhere else.

Rewrite it as classes Standard, Express, and Pickup, each with a name attribute and a cost(weight_kg) method. Then add a fourth class, Drone (a flat $8.00), and a function cheapest(methods, weight_kg) that returns the method with the lowest cost, all without any if on the method's name. Expected output for 3 kg:

Need a hint?

min() takes a key= function: min(methods, key=lambda m: m.cost(weight_kg)) asks each object for its own cost.

Show solution

Adding Drone touched nothing else, and cheapest works for options that don't exist yet. The classes don't even share a parent; duck typing is enough. An ABC would be worth adding once there are several people writing new options and you want a missing cost caught early.

#Exercise 2: One interface, two storage backends

A game saves high scores. Today it uses a dict; next month it should use files. Write an ABC called Storage with abstract methods save(key, value) and load(key), where load raises KeyError for a missing key, and a shared, concrete method load_or(key, default). Implement MemoryStorage (a dict) and FileStorage (one .txt file per key in a folder). This code must work unchanged with both:

Need a hint?

Reading a missing file raises FileNotFoundError, but the interface promises KeyError. Catch one and raise the other with from, or load_or will break for FileStorage only.

Show solution

load_or is written once in the ABC and works for both, because both keep the same promise about KeyError. A backend that raised a different exception would technically have a load method yet still break callers. Matching the method names isn't enough; the behavior has to match too.

#Exercise 3: Let the tests find the bug

This function should turn a title into a URL-friendly slug. Write at least four unittest tests from the examples in its docstring, run them, and fix whatever they reveal.

Need a hint?

Two of the four examples fail. Look at what happens to ", " in 'Hello, World!': two characters that aren't letters, so two spaces.

Show solution

With the original code, the punctuation and spaces tests failed with 'hello--world' != 'hello-world' and 'big---news' != 'big-news'. str.split() with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty pieces, so joining with "-" gives exactly one hyphen between words.

#Exercise 4: Test with a fake clock and a fake notifier

ReminderService texts guests whose check-in is tomorrow. Testing it with the real date would give different results every day. Write a FakeClock with a today() method that returns a fixed date, a FakeNotifier that records messages, and three tests using setUp: only tomorrow's guests get a message, send_reminders returns how many were sent, and an empty list sends nothing.

Need a hint?

The service never asks what kind of clock it has, only that it has today(). Your fake can be three lines long. Make setUp build the clock, the notifier, and the service.

Show solution

Because the clock is passed in rather than created inside the class with date.today(), the tests control time. That's a design choice you make for testability, and it costs one constructor parameter.

#Exercise 5: Make the spec pass

These tests are the whole specification for a club Waitlist. Write Waitlist, AlreadyWaiting, and EmptyWaitlist so that all five pass. Don't change the tests.

Need a hint?

Read each test as a sentence about behavior. len(self.waitlist) needs __len__. The last line of test_joining_twice_is_refused checks that a refused join leaves the list unchanged, so raise before appending.

Show solution

The tests decided the method names, the 1-based positions, and the exception classes before any code existed. That's what test-first means in practice: the caller's view of the interface comes first.

#Exercise 6: The same spec in pytest

In VS Code, rewrite Exercise 5's tests in pytest style. Use a fixture called waitlist that returns a list with Ana, Ben, and Cy, a parametrize table for the three positions, and pytest.raises for both exceptions. Run python -m pytest -v and aim for six passing tests.

Need a hint?

A fixture is a function decorated with @pytest.fixture that returns the object. Any test that takes a parameter with the same name receives a fresh one.

Show solution

To keep this file self-contained, the Waitlist code from Exercise 5 sits at the top; in a project you'd import it instead.

The fixture replaces setUp, and each parametrize row shows up as its own named test, so a wrong position for Ben would be reported as test_position_is_one_based[Ben-2].

#Challenge: A password policy you can extend without editing

Write an ABC Rule with an abstract method problem(password) -> str | None (a message if the rule is broken, None if it's fine). Implement MinLength(n), HasDigit(), and NotCommon(words). Then write PasswordPolicy(rules) with a method problems(password) that returns every message. Add a fourth rule, NoSpaces(), without editing PasswordPolicy, and write unittest tests for a strong password, a weak one that breaks three rules, and the new rule.

Need a hint?

problems is a one-line list comprehension: ask every rule for its problem(password) and keep the ones that aren't None.

Show solution

PasswordPolicy never changed when NoSpaces arrived; it only depends on the Rule interface. That property, open to new behavior without editing old code, has a name you'll meet in the next module: the open/closed principle. The := in problems (the "walrus" operator) stores each rule's message so it's computed once and then tested.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Define refactoring precisely and explain why tests must come first.
  • Name common code smells and the standard refactoring that fixes each.
  • Apply extract function and named constants, and check that the output is unchanged.
  • Explain each SOLID principle with a concrete Python example, and know when not to apply it.

Your teacher likes the quiz report your program prints and asks for one small change: "Can I also get it as a CSV file for the gradebook?" Here's the function.

It works. But every calculation is tangled up with a print, so a CSV version means copying the whole function and changing the output parts. Then there are two copies of the grading rules, and the next time the A cutoff changes, one of them will be missed. The code isn't wrong; it's hard to change. That's what this lesson is about.

#Refactoring means same behavior, better shape

Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing what it does. Same inputs, same outputs, same errors; only the inside moves. Fixing a bug isn't refactoring, and neither is adding a feature. Keeping those separate is the main discipline: refactor first to make the change easy, then make the change.

How do you know the behavior didn't change? You don't, unless something checks. So refactoring starts with tests that pin down what the code does now, even the odd parts. These are called characterization tests. Then you work in small steps (one rename, one extracted function) and rerun the tests after each one. If a test goes red, the last small step is the culprit, and you undo it.

#Smells: signs that a change will hurt

A code smell is a surface pattern that usually means a deeper design problem. It isn't a bug, and a smell is sometimes fine. But each one has a well-known refactoring, with a name you can look up:

Smell What it looks like Usual refactoring
Long function One function does several jobs; you scroll to read it Extract Function
Duplicated code The same rule written twice (the average, above) Extract Function, then call it from both places
Magic numbers 90, * 10, 0.8 with no name Replace Magic Number with Named Constant
Data clumps The same 3 or 4 values passed around together Introduce Parameter Object (often a dataclass)
Primitive obsession Dicts and strings standing in for real concepts Extract Class
Type switch if q["type"] == "mc": ... elif ... in several functions Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
Feature envy A method that mostly uses another object's data Move Method to that object

print_report has the first three. Here it is after extracting functions and naming the numbers. The last line checks that the old and new versions print exactly the same text, which is a characterization test in its simplest form.

The averaging rule exists once, in percent. The grading rule exists once, in letter. And the CSV the teacher asked for took a three-line function, because summarize does the math without printing anything.

#SOLID, one small example at a time

SOLID is five design principles collected by Robert C. Martin. Each one is a response to a specific kind of pain, so learn them through the pain, not as rules.

S: Single responsibility. A class or function should have one reason to change. You just applied it: summarize changes when the math changes, print_report and write_csv change when a format changes. Before, all three reasons landed on one function.

O: Open/closed. Code should be open to new behavior without editing what already works. A quiz with several question types is the classic case. Instead of if q["type"] == ... in every function that marks answers, each type is a class with a check method. Step through and watch q.check(r) land in two different classes:

Adding a TrueFalse type next week means writing one new class. score never changes.

L: Liskov substitution. Wherever the code expects a parent class, any subclass must work, keeping the parent's promises. Here a survey question ("How did you like the quiz?") was made a subclass of Question because it looks like one:

score was correct; the subclass broke Question's promise that check returns a bool. The fix isn't a try in score. It's admitting a survey question isn't a Question: give it its own class, kept in a separate list.

I: Interface segregation. Don't force a class to depend on methods it doesn't use. If a QuizItem ABC demanded check, time_limit, and hint, a simple reflection prompt would need three methods that raise NotImplementedError, which is the Liskov problem again. Several small ABCs (Gradable, Timed) let each class sign up only for what it really does; in Python a class can inherit from more than one.

D: Dependency inversion. High-level code should depend on an interface, not on a specific low-level class. If Quiz.__init__ creates its own FileLeaderboard(), every test writes to a real file. Pass the leaderboard in instead:

The real program passes a FileLeaderboard; tests pass a MemoryLeaderboard and check entries. Quiz doesn't change either way. This is the same move as the fake notifier from the last module, now with a name.

⚠️ Watch out

Changing behavior mid-refactor. You notice a bug while extracting a function and fix it in the same step. Now a test fails and you can't tell whether the refactor broke something or the fix changed expected output. Finish the refactor with tests green, then fix the bug as its own change with its own new test.

⚠️ Watch out

SOLID as a checklist. An ABC with exactly one implementation, created "in case we need another someday", adds a file and a layer of indirection for nothing. Apply a principle when you feel the pain it addresses: a second implementation, a test you can't write, a change that touches five places.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Which of these is a refactoring?

  • The structure changed and the observable behavior didn't. That's the definition.

  • That changes the output; it's a new requirement, not a refactoring.

  • A bug fix changes behavior on purpose. Do it as its own step.

Show answer

A. The structure changed and the observable behavior didn't. That's the definition.

2Three functions each contain if customer_type == "staff": .... Which smell is this, and what's the usual fix?

  • Splitting them would still leave the type check repeated in every function.

  • One class per customer type, each with its own method, puts each type's rules in one place.

  • The repeated problem is the branching on type, not a bare number.

Show answer

B. One class per customer type, each with its own method, puts each type's rules in one place.

3ReadOnlyStorage subclasses Storage and makes save() raise NotImplementedError. Which principle does it break?

  • It might have one job; the problem is how it treats callers.

  • Code written for Storage calls save() and expects it to work, so the subclass can't stand in for its parent.

  • That's about which classes high-level code depends on, not about a subclass breaking promises.

Show answer

B. Code written for Storage calls save() and expects it to work, so the subclass can't stand in for its parent.

4Why pass the leaderboard into Quiz instead of creating it inside __init__?

  • Quiz depends only on "something with record", so the caller chooses the concrete class.

  • Speed isn't the point; flexibility and testability are.

  • Creating objects inside __init__ is allowed; it just welds the classes together.

Show answer

A. Quiz depends only on "something with record", so the caller chooses the concrete class.

Key takeaways

  • Refactoring changes structure, never behavior; pin behavior with characterization tests first, then move in small steps.
  • Smells (long functions, duplication, magic numbers, type switches) predict where changes will hurt, and each has a named fix.
  • Separating calculation from output is often the highest-value first refactor: it makes code testable and reusable.
  • S: one reason to change. O: add behavior by adding classes. L: subclasses keep their parent's promises. I: small interfaces. D: depend on interfaces and pass dependencies in.
  • Don't mix bug fixes with refactoring, and don't add abstractions before something needs them.

  • Code Smells (opens in a new tab) at Refactoring.Guru, grouped by kind, with illustrated explanations of each fix.

m7-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write characterization tests that pin down existing behavior, including a bug.
  • Refactor in small steps: extract function, named constants, extract class, replace conditional with polymorphism.
  • Keep an old entry point working as a thin wrapper while the inside is rebuilt.
  • Fix a bug as a separate, test-first change after the refactor is finished.

The school store's checkout code was written in a hurry before the first spirit week, and it shows. Every new discount was squeezed into one function, the stock rules exist in two places, and the last two changes each broke something that used to work. The treasurer now wants a new "big order" discount. Nobody wants to touch the function.

You'll rebuild it from the inside while keeping its output identical, then add the new discount by writing one small class. Here is where it ends up:

#Step 1: Read the legacy code

This is store.py as it is today. Run it once and read the receipt.

Count the smells: a long function doing five jobs (validate, price, discount, update stock, format), magic numbers (0.2, 0.1, 20, 5), a type switch on order["customer"], the stock rule duplicated in can_buy, and a global STOCK dict that everything mutates.

#Step 2: Pin the behavior before changing anything

Characterization tests describe what the code does now. They compare whole receipts, character for character, because any difference counts as a change. setUp resets the global stock before each test, which is itself a sign of the global-state smell: the tests have to clean up after the code.

Six green tests, and one of them pins a bug: a robotics member buying a 50-cent pencil gets $5 off and the store owes them $4.50. Writing the tests found it. It's tempting to fix it right now. Don't: if you fix it mid-refactor and a test goes red later, you won't know which change caused it. Pin it, note it, keep going.

#Step 3: Extract functions and name the numbers

The first refactor is mechanical: pull each job into a function and give every number a name. checkout becomes a short list of steps.

Still six green. stock_problem now reuses can_buy, so the stock rule exists in one place. Each function can be read, tested, and changed on its own.

#Step 4: Extract an Inventory class with real exceptions

Stock is state with rules attached, which is exactly what a class is for. Inventory owns the dict and raises the custom exceptions from Module 5 instead of returning strings. The old checkout and can_buy stay as thin wrappers, so their callers (and the pinned tests) never notice.

take checks every item before changing any stock, so a failed order leaves the inventory untouched, the same as before. The messages are identical because the exception classes build the same text the old string concatenation did. stock_problem is no longer used; delete it.

#Step 5: Replace the discount conditional with rule classes

The if/elif in discount_for is the part that keeps breaking. Each discount becomes a class with one method, amount, and the customer's two loose values become a small dataclass (the data-clump fix). Since staff and student discounts never both apply, and the club rule was "at least $5", the total discount is simply the largest amount any rule offers.

Green again, bug and all. The negative total survived because this step preserved behavior exactly, which is the point.

#Step 6: An injectable Checkout, and the new discount

Last structural step. Checkout receives its inventory, prices, and rules instead of reaching for globals, so new code (and tests) can build one with any stock and any rules. The legacy checkout() becomes a short adapter.

Now the treasurer's request. A big-order discount is one new class; nothing that already works gets edited. And because Checkout takes its dependencies, this demo uses its own inventory and never touches the global STOCK:

The guest's $51 order gets the $6 big-order discount. The staff member's $50 order qualifies too, but 20% ($10) is bigger, so the staff rule wins. "Best single discount" is now one line in Checkout.run, so if the store ever decides discounts should stack, that one line is the only place to change.

#Step 7: Fix the bug, as its own change

With the refactor finished and green, fix the negative total. Test first, and notice what the refactor bought you: the club rule is now a small class you can test directly, without building a whole order.

Red, for the right reason: 5.0 != 0.5. The fix is one expression, in the one place the rule lives:

The two new tests pass, and exactly one old test fails: test_tiny_robotics_order_goes_negative, the one that pinned the bug. That failure is the good kind. It proves the fix changed the behavior you meant to change and nothing else. Delete that test from test_store.py; the new unit test now describes the correct behavior.

#The finished store.py

Here is the whole module after all seven steps, with the big-order rule added to the defaults, followed by one last run of every test (minus the deleted one).

The last two lines are for this page only: del removes the pinned-bug test from the class, just as you deleted it from the file. Every remaining receipt test passes against the finished module, so for every order the tests cover, it prints exactly what the legacy code printed.

⚠️ Watch out

Big-bang rewrites. It's tempting to delete the legacy function and write Checkout from scratch. Then nothing tells you whether the new code matches the old receipts, and edge cases (like take checking every item before changing any stock) quietly disappear. Each step above was small enough to undo in seconds, and the pinned tests ran after every one.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did Step 2 pin the negative-total bug instead of fixing it immediately?

  • They can; Step 7 changes the test to do exactly that.

  • Mixing them makes a red test ambiguous: was it the refactor or the fix?

  • It isn't; but even real bugs get fixed as their own step.

Show answer

B. Mixing them makes a red test ambiguous: was it the refactor or the fix?

2Why does the legacy checkout(order) function still exist at the end?

  • Keeping the old entry point lets you refactor the inside without breaking any caller.

  • Callers can create and use Checkout directly; the adapter is for old callers.

  • It does slightly more work, since it builds a Checkout on each call.

Show answer

A. Keeping the old entry point lets you refactor the inside without breaking any caller.

3The store decides discounts should stack: staff get 20% and the big-order $6. How many places change?

  • The rules each report their own amount; they don't decide how amounts combine.

  • How amounts combine is the checkout's job, and it lives in exactly one expression.

  • Neither knows anything about discounts.

Show answer

B. How amounts combine is the checkout's job, and it lives in exactly one expression.

Key takeaways

  • Pin current behavior with characterization tests before refactoring, and compare whole outputs.
  • Refactor in steps small enough to undo: extract function, name constants, extract class, replace conditional with polymorphism, inject dependencies.
  • Keep old entry points as thin adapters so callers don't break while the inside changes.
  • Polymorphic rule classes turn "add a discount" into "add a class", leaving tested code alone.
  • Fix bugs after the refactor, test first, in the one place the rule now lives.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Make receipt a method of a Receipt class and add a to_csv() alongside it, with tests for both.
  • Add a Prices class that raises UnknownItem for a missing SKU, and remove the separate PRICES dict from Checkout.
  • Split store.py into a package (store/errors.py, store/inventory.py, store/discounts.py, store/checkout.py) using the import direction rule from Module 5.

#Further reading

  • Replace Conditional with Polymorphism (opens in a new tab), Martin Fowler's catalog entry for the move in Step 5.
  • Refactoring techniques (opens in a new tab) at Refactoring.Guru, organized by what kind of mess each technique cleans up.

What you'll learn

  • Prove a refactor kept behavior identical by comparing old and new code over many inputs.
  • Apply named constants, extract function, introduce parameter object, and replace conditional with polymorphism.
  • Repair a subclass that breaks its parent's promises.
  • Make code that depends on randomness testable by passing the dependency in.

Every exercise here starts from code that works. Your job is to change its shape without changing its behavior, so each solution ends with a check that old and new agree. Keep the original as old_... in the same file while you work; that's your characterization test for free.

#Warm-up: name the smells

Before reading on, list every smell you can find in this function.

Cryptic names (u, s, "t"); primitive obsession, since a user is a dict of one-letter keys; a type switch on u["t"]; duplicated formatting of name and email in every branch; magic numbers (1, 10); and a latent crash, because an unknown plan leaves s unassigned and raises UnboundLocalError.

#Exercise 1: Name the numbers, extract the repetition

Replace every number with a named constant, and extract one overage(used, included, rate) function that replaces the three look-alike if blocks. Then prove nothing changed: compare the old and new bill on every combination of a few thousand inputs.

Need a hint?

itertools.product(range(0, 1000, 50), range(0, 1200, 100), range(12)) gives you every combination of three ranges. all(old_bill(*u) == bill(*u) for u in ...) checks them in one line.

Show solution

overage encodes the one rule the three blocks shared ("only what's over the allowance costs extra"), and the constants put every number the phone company might change in one place. Comparing thousands of inputs catches mistakes a handful of hand-picked tests would miss.

#Exercise 2: Introduce a parameter object

Six loose values travel together through clashes. Introduce a frozen dataclass Slot(day, start, end) with an overlaps method and a __str__, and a Booking(room, slot). Moving the clash test onto Slot also fixes a feature-envy smell: the function only ever used a slot's data.

Expected output, unchanged: Clash: Lab: Mon 9:00-11:00 and Lab: Mon 10:00-12:00

Need a hint?

Give Booking a method clashes_with(other) that checks the room and then delegates to self.slot.overlaps(other.slot).

Show solution

The loop no longer unpacks tuples with *slot_a, and nobody can pass a start and end in the wrong order without it being obvious, because they're named fields.

#Exercise 3: Replace the format switch with classes

Write one class per format, each with export(rows) -> str, and a dict EXPORTERS mapping names to instances. Keep export(rows, fmt) as a thin wrapper (it must still raise ValueError for an unknown format). Then add tab-separated output by writing a single new class.

Need a hint?

The wrapper becomes a dictionary lookup inside try/except KeyError, re-raising as ValueError ... from None so callers see the same error type as before.

Show solution

TsvExporter inherits everything from CsvExporter and changes one class attribute. That's inheritance used well: a TSV file really is a CSV file with a different separator, so every promise the parent makes still holds. from None hides the internal KeyError from the traceback, because it's an implementation detail.

#Exercise 4: The square that broke the rectangle

stretch was written for rectangles and assumes that setting the width leaves the height alone. Run it with a Square:

Restructure the classes so this can't happen: a shared Shape ABC with area(), and Rectangle and Square as separate, immutable (frozen dataclass) implementations. stretch should return a new Rectangle instead of mutating one.

Need a hint?

A square can't keep the promise "changing width doesn't change height", so it shouldn't inherit it. The only promise the two really share is "I have an area".

Show solution

Code that needs "any shape" takes Shape and only calls area(), which both keep. Code that needs width and height takes Rectangle, and a Square can't be passed in by accident. Immutability removes the setters, which were the promise Square couldn't keep.

#Exercise 5: Inject the randomness

A 5% chance of a dragon egg is nearly impossible to test when the function calls random.random() itself:

Change it to open_chest(rng), where rng is anything with a .random() method. The game passes random.Random(); tests pass a FakeRng that returns chosen numbers. Write unittest tests for all three outcomes and for both boundaries (exactly 0.05 and exactly 0.30).

Need a hint?

FakeRng needs only __init__(self, value) and random(self). Test boundaries deliberately; that's where < versus <= bugs hide.

Show solution

The real game stays random, a seeded random.Random(7) gives the same sequence on every run (handy for reproducing a player's bug report), and the tests are exact. This is dependency inversion again: open_chest depends on "something with random()", not on the random module.

#Exercise 6: Pin down code you don't understand

Nobody remembers why member codes are computed this way, but codes are printed on cards that are already in people's wallets, so the output must never change.

First, run it on at least six varied names (short, punctuated, mixed case, a single letter) and save the results as a dict of expected codes. That dict is your characterization test. Then rewrite the function with readable helpers and prove every expected code still matches.

Need a hint?

You don't need to understand why the formula exists to preserve it. Translate it piece by piece: letters only, pad to three, a weighted sum of letter positions, two-digit remainder.

Show solution

The pinned dict caught every subtle detail you might have "tidied" by accident, such as the checksum using all the letters rather than just the first three. str.ljust(3, "X") pads only when the string is shorter, exactly like the original if.

#Challenge: Turn a command switch into command classes

This handler for a tiny text adventure has an if/elif branch per command, and it'll keep growing. Refactor it into a Command ABC with a names tuple and run(args, state) -> str, one class per command, and a Registry that maps every name (including the "i" shortcut) to its command. handle should become a lookup. Prove the replies are identical for the script below, then add a Drop command without editing the registry.

Need a hint?

Read the original closely: look and inventory ignore any extra words, but go and take only match with exactly one word after them; otherwise they fall through to "I don't understand that." Give each command an arity, with None meaning "any number of words", so the registry can preserve that quirk.

Show solution

The comparison checks the final game state as well as every reply, since a command could print the right text and still update the wrong thing. Preserving the arity quirk exactly is the refactor; making look strict about extra words would be a separate, deliberate change with its own test. This command structure is also the backbone of the capstone's adventure engine.

m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Choose a capstone project at the right size and list the requirements it must meet.
  • Turn a plain-language scenario into classes, responsibilities, and collaborators.
  • Draw a class diagram and a sequence diagram, and justify each composition or inheritance link.
  • Write an acceptance test before any real code, and plan milestones that each end with something working.

Most capstone projects that fail don't fail at the code. They fail on day one, when someone starts typing class Game: with no idea what the other classes will be, and three days later every class knows about every other class. One afternoon of planning prevents that. By the end of this lesson you'll have a design document, a class diagram, and one failing test that says exactly what "finished" means.

#What your application must include

Your capstone is a command-line Python application of your own design. It must show the skills from Modules 2 to 7, at least at this level:

Requirement Minimum Learned in
Classes with clear jobs 5 or more, each describable in one sentence Module 2
Composition At least 2 "has-a" relationships Module 3
Inheritance or an interface An abc.ABC (or duck-typed interface) with 2+ implementations used polymorphically Modules 3, 6
Protected state Validation in constructors or properties; no outside code reaching into _private attributes Module 4
Custom exceptions A base class and 2+ subclasses, caught at one boundary Module 5
Package layout 3+ modules in a package, started with python -m yourpackage Module 5
Type hints On every public method's parameters and return value Modules 4, 5
Tests 12+ unit tests, including error paths and at least one fake or fixture Module 6
A refactor One documented before-and-after improvement, tests green throughout Module 7
Design document Diagram, responsibilities, and justified relationships (template below) This lesson

#Five project ideas

Pick one, or propose your own of similar size. The difficulty is about how many moving parts the design has, not how much code you type.

Project Difficulty Core classes Where polymorphism lives
Library loans Starter Book, Copy, Member, Loan, Library Notifier (email, console, fake) for due-date reminders; reuse DateRange
Text adventure engine Medium Room, Item, Player, World, Game, Command One class per command (Look, Go, Take, ...) behind a Command ABC
Habit tracker Medium Habit, CheckIn, Streak, Tracker Storage ABC with JSON and in-memory backends; Schedule (daily, weekdays, weekly)
Turn-based arena Medium-hard Fighter, Move, StatusEffect, Team, Battle Move and StatusEffect subclasses (heal, poison, shield) that each change a fighter differently
Elevator simulation Hard Elevator, Floor, Request, Building, Scheduler Swappable Scheduler strategies (nearest-first, sweep), compared by average wait time

The next lesson builds a starter for the text adventure engine, so the examples here use it. Every technique applies to the other projects.

#Find the classes: nouns, verbs, and responsibilities

Write a short paragraph describing your program from the user's side, the way you'd explain it to a friend. Then underline the nouns and the verbs.

The player starts in the hall of an old house. Each room has a description, some exits, and sometimes items. The player can look around, go in a direction, take and drop items, and check their inventory. Some doors are locked and need a key to unlock. Reaching the vault wins the game.

Nouns are candidate classes or attributes; verbs are candidate methods. Not every noun becomes a class. "Description" is just a string attribute of Room, and "door" turns out to be a locked exit, not an object of its own. The test is whether the noun has behavior or rules of its own.

Then write a CRC card (Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators) for each class that survives. If you can't state a class's responsibility in one sentence, it's doing too much.

Class Responsibility (one sentence) Collaborators
Room Knows its description, its exits, which exits are locked, and the items lying in it. Item
Item Holds an item's name and description. none
Player Tracks where the player is and what they carry, and moves between rooms. Room, Item
World Builds all the rooms from map data and finds them by name. Room, Item
Command (ABC) Turns one typed command into a change to the game and a reply. Game
Game Reads a line, picks the command, catches game errors, and knows when the player has won. World, Player, Command

#Draw it before you build it

A class diagram shows the structure; a sequence diagram shows one interaction over time. You need both, but only for the core of the program.

Drawing the sequence first often reveals a missing method: here, Room.remove_item has to exist, and it's the place to raise CantDoThat when the item isn't there.

#Composition or inheritance? Write down why

For every line on your diagram, write one sentence of justification. Inheritance needs the strongest case: the child must keep every promise the parent makes (Liskov, Module 7).

Relationship Kind Why
Game has a World and a Player Composition A game is made of these parts; neither is a kind of game.
Room holds Items Aggregation Items exist on their own and move between rooms and the inventory.
Go is a Command Inheritance from an ABC Every command keeps the same promise, run(game, args) -> str, and Game treats them all alike.
Player is not a subclass of Room (rejected) It would get exits and descriptions it can't use; the player is in a room.

#Write the acceptance test first

An acceptance test checks the whole program from the user's point of view. Writing it now turns a vague goal ("make a game") into a precise one, using the interface from your diagram. Stub the class so the test can run, and watch it fail:

Two errors, and that's the plan working. These tests will stay red through the early milestones and turn green in Milestone 4. Notice the decisions they already forced: the world is plain data (so a map can live in a JSON file), handle returns the reply as a string instead of printing it (so tests can read it), and winning is a property of Game.

#Your design document

Keep this as DESIGN.md in your project folder and update it as the design changes. Reviewers read it before your code.

#Plan milestones that each end with something working

Each milestone ends with a program you can run and tests that pass. If you run out of time, you hand in the last finished milestone, not a half-built pile.

A walking skeleton (M1) is the thinnest version that runs end to end: two rooms, look, go, and a loop. It feels too small to bother with. Build it anyway: it proves your classes fit together before you've invested in any of them.

💡 Tip

Scope down early. If the arena or elevator idea feels big, cut features, not structure: two kinds of Move instead of six, one scheduling strategy plus a fake. The rubric rewards clear design and tests, not feature count.

#Before you start building

  • I picked a project and wrote the user-side paragraph.
  • Every class has a one-sentence responsibility and listed collaborators.
  • I have a class diagram and one sequence diagram.
  • Every relationship has a written justification.
  • My acceptance test runs and fails for the right reason.
  • DESIGN.md exists with every heading from the template.
  • My milestones each end with something that runs.
